channel.title: Anshuman Mishra
channel.description: Machine learning engineer building AI systems, open source software, and essays.

item.title: Let the small model prefill
item.description:
In How do we transfer context between models?, OneTriangle explore an interesting idea: a smaller model like Qwen3.5-4B can handle prefill for a bigger model. Since the smaller model needs less compute, this can save a lot of prefill time.

That got me thinking: if a smaller model can handle prefill, we could do that work with a smaller compute budget and fit in more requests. That could help boost throughput for a given amount of compute.

I wanted to see whether this idea works in practice, so I started by reproducing the recipe. From there, I tried a few different model pairs and ways of sharing the work:

  • Reproduce the recipe on a simpler Qwen model pair and see whether it works
  • Do keys or values matter more for the transferred cache?
  • Can this work with a hybrid DeltaNet model?
  • What happens if I transfer only some layers?
  • What if the big model reads the end of the prompt itself?
  • Does it hold up on long contexts?
  • Can a dense model prefill for a mixture of experts?
  • What happens across model families and tokenizers?

Before getting into those experiments, here is a quick primer on the KV cache and what gets transferred.

A quick primer on KV cache

Generating a response has two parts: prefill and decode.

During prefill, the model processes the prompt tokens. In each attention layer, it computes queries, keys and values. Each token uses its query to attend to the keys and values of the tokens it is allowed to see. The model saves the keys and values for the prompt in a KV cache, and uses the prefill output to predict the first response token.

During decode, the model generates the rest of the response one token at a time. At each step, it processes the latest token and computes its query, key and value. It uses the new query to attend to the cached keys and values from the prompt and earlier generated tokens, then adds the new key and value to the cache. That way it can use the earlier context without recomputing its keys and values at every step.

For a long prompt, prefill can take a while because the model has to process all those prompt tokens before it starts generating. A bigger model generally needs more compute for that work. The idea behind cache transfer is to let a smaller model do that reading, then use a learned mapper to turn its states into a cache the bigger model can use.

The recipe: a small model reads for a big model

OneTriangle describe this recipe in their cache-transfer post. To reproduce it, we freeze both models and train a mapper: a set of linear maps that turns the small model’s states into keys and values for the big model’s cache. We build separate maps for the keys and values of each target layer. The layer-selection method and settings below describe our implementation.

Stage 1: fit a direct map

First, we run both models on the same text and collect the keys and values their layers produce. For each big-model layer, we test how well each small-model layer can predict its keys. We use ridge regression to fit a linear map: it looks for a close match while keeping the map’s weights from becoming too large. We select the three small-model layers with the lowest prediction error, combine their outputs, and fit a new map using all three. We repeat the process separately for values.

The picture below follows one of those maps. Each block represents a layer; the counts are illustrative. The highlighted small-model layers supply the input for one big-model layer. We repeat this for every target layer to build its cache.

We can use this ridge map as it is. In the Qwen3-0.6B → Qwen3-8B reproduction below, it reaches a KL of 0.42, compared with 0.73 when the big model gets no prefix. That is a useful starting point, but there is still room to improve.

Stage 2: train a correction

Next, we improve the ridge map by adding a trainable correction: W = W₀ + A·B. The two smaller matrices A and B let us adjust the map without training a full new matrix. Their product has rank 64, and B starts at zero, so training begins with the ridge map.

We start with documents from FineWeb-Edu and tokenize them before training. We keep documents long enough for the largest split: at least 2,176 tokens. At each training step, we choose a prefix length between 512 and 2,048 tokens and sample documents from the training set. For each document, we take that many tokens from the beginning as the prefix, then take the next 128 tokens as the continuation. The prefix gives the models context, and the continuation gives us a way to compare their predictions.

The teacher is the big model processing both parts with its own cache. For the student, the small model reads the prefix and the mapper builds a cache for it; the big model then processes the continuation using that mapped cache. We compare what the teacher and student predict at each continuation position, and train the correction to bring those predictions closer using KL divergence. Both language models remain frozen.

We use AdamW at a learning rate of 2e-4, with 8 documents per step for 1,000–1,500 steps. At inference, the maps use bf16. In the same Qwen reproduction, this second stage brings KL down from 0.42 to 0.13.

Before looking at the results, let’s walk through how we evaluate each model pair.

  • Next-token distribution agreement. We give the big model a 2,048-token prefix and a 128-token continuation from each of 64 held-out FineWeb-Edu documents. We compare its next-token probability distributions when it uses the transferred prefix cache against when it builds the prefix cache itself. We report KL divergence, where lower means the distributions are closer, and top-1 agreement, where higher means the two runs more often assign the highest probability to the same token.
  • Task accuracy. We evaluate on SQuAD (300 questions, with the relevant paragraph hidden among distractors, about 4.2k tokens), HotpotQA (300 questions, with distractor documents padded to about 4.5k tokens), and GSM8K (400 questions, with eight worked examples in each prompt, about 1.1k tokens). The documents or worked examples make up the prefix whose cache we transfer. We feed the question header to the big model normally.
  • Prefill time. We measure elapsed prefill time for one request at a time and report the best of three runs, unless stated otherwise.

The early reproduction uses 128 held-out documents for fidelity; later runs use 64. The long-context experiments also have their own task settings, which we’ll cover when we get there.

Experiment 0: reproducing the recipe on Qwen3-0.6B → Qwen3-8B

We start with a simple transformer architecture that uses attention layers throughout. We choose Qwen3-0.6B as the small model and Qwen3-8B as the big model, and try the cache-transfer recipe on this pair before moving on to hybrid models.

First, we use the direct weight mapping from Stage 1 to build the 8B’s prefix KV cache. We then feed the continuation to the 8B and record its next-token probability distributions. As a reference, we run the same continuation after letting the 8B build its own prefix cache. The average KL divergence between the two runs is 0.42. For another comparison, we run the 8B on the continuation without giving it the prefix or a prefix cache. Comparing that run’s next-token distributions with the reference run, where the 8B reads the prefix itself, gives a KL of 0.73. After we train the correction in Stage 2, the KL drops to 0.13, meaning the next-token distributions are closer to those from the 8B’s own cache. This metric compares token probabilities, not the KV values directly.

Let’s look at what these results tell us.

  1. The transferred cache preserves more information for SQuAD than for the reasoning tasks. With Qwen3-0.6B doing prefill and the 8B answering, SQuAD F1 is 0.721, close to 0.738 when the 8B builds its own cache. On HotpotQA, F1 drops from 0.603 to 0.461; on GSM8K, accuracy drops from 0.925 to 0.665.
  2. We also need to compare against the small model answering on its own. For example, when Qwen3-4B does prefill and the 8B answers using its cache, GSM8K accuracy is 0.877. But the 4B answers correctly 0.915 of the time on its own. In this case, adding the mapper and the 8B does not improve the score.

We also repeat the round-3 run on a different machine using the same command. The average KL divergence between the 8B’s next-token distributions changes from 0.128 to 0.129. Task scores vary by about 0.02–0.04 between independent training runs, so we should keep that variation in mind when comparing the results below.

Experiment 1: which matters more, keys or values?

The first experiment tells us that the transferred cache changes the 8B’s next-token distributions. But the cache contains two different things: keys and values. We want to know which part contributes more to that change for Qwen3-0.6B → Qwen3-8B.

We use the rank-16 mapper trained in Experiment 0. To see how mapped keys and mapped values each affect the 8B’s next-token distributions, we run the 8B with three versions of the prefix KV cache:

  1. Keys and values mapped from 0.6B: use the mapper to build both parts of the cache.
  2. 8B keys, values mapped from 0.6B: use the keys the 8B produces when it reads the prefix, and map the values from 0.6B.
  3. Keys mapped from 0.6B, 8B values: map the keys from 0.6B, and use the values the 8B produces when it reads the prefix.

For each cache, we feed the continuation to the 8B and compare its next-token probability distributions with the distributions from the 8B reading the full prefix itself. We use 128 held-out FineWeb-Edu documents, with a 2,048-token prefix and a 128-token continuation. Lower KL divergence means the distributions are closer to the reference.

Prefix cache used by the 8B KL divergence Top-1 agreement
Keys and values mapped from 0.6B 0.135 0.842
8B keys, values mapped from 0.6B 0.134 0.844
Keys mapped from 0.6B, 8B values 0.094 0.876

Replacing the mapped keys barely changes the KL: 0.135 becomes 0.134. Replacing the mapped values brings it down to 0.094. In this test, the 8B’s own values help its next-token distributions more than its own keys do. OneTriangle reported the opposite for their model pairs, so we should not assume the same result for every pair.

Experiment 2: partial-layer transfer

The transferred cache works well on SQuAD, but the 8B loses accuracy on the reasoning tasks. This raises a question: can we recover some of that accuracy by letting the 8B process part of the prompt itself?

So far, we have transferred keys and values for every layer. This time, we let the 8B compute some layers during prefill and use mapped keys and values for the others. We can then compare how different choices affect accuracy and prefill time.

For each layer we transfer, we skip the 8B’s layer computation and put the mapped keys and values into its cache. But there is another piece to handle: if the 8B needs to compute a layer after a group of skipped layers, it also needs a hidden state to pass into that layer. We train a second map, Δ, to estimate how the skipped layers would have changed that hidden state.

We try different choices of layers to transfer. For each choice, we fit new initial maps and train them for 1,500 steps using the same KL-based method as Experiment 0.

Here’s what we see when we change which layers the 8B computes:

Keeping the first layers on the 8B improves GSM8K accuracy. The 8B processes its 36 layers in order, from first to last. In these runs, we let it compute the first layers and transfer the cache for the last layers:

First layers computed by the 8B Last layers transferred from 0.6B GSM8K accuracy (% of 8B with its own cache) Prefill speedup
6 30 69% 2.4×
15 21 76% 1.55×
18 18 88% 1.35×
21 15 94% 1.23×
24 12 97% 1.14×

When we reverse the split and transfer the first 18 layers instead, GSM8K accuracy falls to 13% of the 8B’s accuracy with its own cache.

  • Keeping 15–18 of the 36 layers on the 8B gives us a useful trade-off. We recover much of the GSM8K accuracy while still reducing prefill time. With fewer than about nine layers computed by the 8B, the tested plans stay close to the accuracy of transferring every layer, but add the cost of running those layers.
  • The layer we start with matters for the interleaved plans we tested. Transferring every other layer while letting the 8B compute layer 0 gives 87% of the 8B’s GSM8K accuracy at a 1.31× prefill speedup. Keeping every other layer but transferring layer 0 gives 59%. Layer 0 contains the attention sink, so sensitivity to errors there may be one reason for the gap.
  • The Δ map matters when we skip layers. Without it, the tested interleaved plans reach around 50% of the 8B’s score on each task. They perform worse than transferring every layer, at a similar prefill speed.

These timings come from Qwen3-0.6B → Qwen3-8B in Hugging Face. The small model and the mapper account for a sizeable part of the work in this pair. The trade-off could look different with a larger target model, where running each layer may cost more.

Experiment 3: letting the big model read the tail

In Experiment 2, letting the 8B compute more layers improved accuracy, but reduced the prefill speedup. Now we try a different split: the 0.6B reads most of the prompt, and the 8B reads the final part itself using the mapped cache for the earlier tokens. We call that final part the native tail.

In an earlier run, letting the 8B read the last 512 tokens reduced the average KL divergence between next-token distributions from 0.135 to 0.047. To see how this affects task scores and speed, we combine six layer plans from Experiment 2 with five tail sizes: none, 1/32, 1/16, 1/8, and 1/4 of the prompt. We evaluate each combination on the same 300 SQuAD, 300 HotpotQA, and 400 GSM8K questions.

We express the tail as a fraction so it scales with the length of each prompt. We use the existing Experiment 2 mappers without retraining them; the 8B reads the tail at inference time.

Here’s what we see when we vary the layers and the tail:

  • A short tail improves GSM8K accuracy in this setup. With every layer transferred and no tail, the 8B reaches 70% of its own GSM8K accuracy. Letting it read the last 1/16 of the prompt raises that to 96%, with a 2.5× prefill speedup at 8k tokens. The layer-only plan with similar accuracy, last:12, gives a 1.12× speedup. Here, the math question is near the end of the transferred prompt: its median length is 5.3% of the prompt. A 1/16 tail covers the whole question in two thirds of the prompts. A 1/32 tail covers the whole question in only 6% of prompts, but still raises accuracy to 87% of the 8B’s.
  • The tail does not improve the all-transferred HotpotQA result. It stays at 74% of the 8B’s score across the tail sizes. The 8B already reads the question header in this setup, while the documents remain transferred. Letting the 8B compute more layers raises the score to 89% with last:12; adding a tail raises it to as much as 94%.
  • SQuAD changes little across the combinations. Scores stay between 91% and 95% of the 8B’s score.
  • The cost of the tail depends on context length. With every layer transferred and a 1/4 tail, prefill is 1.75× faster at 8k tokens and 1.40× faster at 32k. At 2k tokens, the tested tails bring speedup down to 0.8–1.0×. Our implementation processes the tail in a second forward pass, which adds fixed overhead; a serving implementation could potentially reduce that overhead.

For these prompts, letting the 8B read the final part helps most when it contains information the 8B needs to handle directly, as with the GSM8K questions. For HotpotQA, where the relevant information is spread across the transferred documents, computing more layers is more useful in this experiment.

Experiment 4: a hybrid big model (Qwen3.5-4B → Qwen3.8-27B)

So far, we have used two Qwen3 models with attention layers throughout. Now we move to the pair from the OneTriangle post: Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.8-27B. Both are hybrid models: three out of every four layers use Gated DeltaNet, while the remaining layers use full attention.

The full-attention layers keep keys and values for each prefix token, which we can map as before. DeltaNet layers need a different approach. Instead of keeping a per-token KV cache, each layer maintains two fixed-size states:

  • A recurrent state, which the layer updates as it processes tokens and uses when processing the next token.
  • A convolution state, which holds the recent inputs needed by the layer’s short causal convolution.

These states do not grow with the length of the prefix. During decoding, the layer continues updating them as it processes new tokens.

Building the DeltaNet states

Rather than predict these states directly, we map the 4B’s hidden states to an estimate of the input to each 27B DeltaNet layer. We then use the 27B’s own DeltaNet computation to build the states from that estimated input. The diagram follows this path for one layer; the Algorithm and Code tabs show the steps in more detail.

Next, we compare task scores for the 27B using its own cache, the 27B using the transferred cache, and the 4B answering on its own:

method SQuAD F1 HotpotQA F1 GSM8K
Qwen3.8-27B itself 0.929 0.775 0.907
Qwen3.5-4B prefill → transfer 0.797 (86%) 0.717 (93%) 0.868 (96%)
Qwen3.5-4B alone 0.897 (97%) 0.720 (93%) 0.855 (94%)
27B, closed book 0.301 0.329 –

On these QA tasks, the 4B answering on its own scores about as well as or better than the 27B using the transferred cache. On GSM8K, transfer scores 0.868 against the 4B’s 0.855. To see whether the larger model offers more of an advantage on longer contexts, we turn to long-context evaluation next.

Experiment 5: long-context prefill, 8k to 248k tokens

The short-context results left me with another question: would transfer be more useful when the prompt gets really long? Long contexts are also where saving prefill time could matter most. I wanted to see how much time transfer saves as the prompt grows, and whether it still works beyond the mapper’s training length of at most 2k tokens.

I built a dedicated benchmark (make_long_data.py) with two parts:

  • Needle in a haystack: 20 prompts at each of 8k, 16k, 32k, 64k, 128k and 248k tokens, each with 4 keys to retrieve. This checks retrieval.
  • LongBench v2: 100 questions of up to 120k tokens, sampled with seed 0. These are 4-way multiple-choice questions that need reasoning over the whole document, so they actually separate strong models from weak ones.

For timing I measured two things. The first is the full transfer pipeline in HuggingFace, end to end. The second is native time to first token in SGLang for both models. SGLang has no transfer path yet, so its 27B ÷ 4B ratio is the ceiling an optimised implementation could approach.

Most of the gap between the measured 2.2–2.4× and the 4–6× ceiling is the DeltaNet state fill. The 27B still runs its 48 DeltaNet kernels over the full prompt, just without their outputs. That is why the transfer pipeline costs about 1.75× the 4B prefill alone (8.4 s vs 4.8 s at 128k).

Now let’s compare answer quality. For LongBench v2, we report the fraction of 100 questions answered correctly. For the needle test, we report retrieval accuracy across prompts from 8k to 248k tokens, with 20 prompts at each length.

Prompt processing Answering model LongBench v2 accuracy Needle retrieval accuracy
Qwen3.8-27B Qwen3.8-27B 52% 100%
Qwen3.5-4B, with its cache mapped to the 27B Qwen3.8-27B 50% 100% at every length
Qwen3.5-4B Qwen3.5-4B 39% 100%

The LongBench v2 results show the clearest difference between the three setups. The 27B answers 52 of the 100 questions correctly when it reads the prompt itself, and 50 when it uses the transferred cache. The 4B answering on its own gets 39. With only 100 questions, we should be cautious about drawing conclusions from the small gap between the two 27B runs.

On the needle test, the 27B retrieves every needle using the transferred cache, including at 248k tokens. That is well beyond the mapper’s training prefixes of at most 2k tokens. But the 4B answering on its own also retrieves every needle, so this test does not show whether transfer improves retrieval. The LongBench length breakdown gives us a more useful next step: train the mapper on longer prefixes and test whether that improves the results beyond 64k tokens.

Experiment 6: dense → MoE (Qwen3.5-4B → Qwen3.5-35B-A3B)

The hybrid model worked, so I wanted to see if transfer would also work when the larger model was a mixture of experts (MoE). I tried transferring from a dense model to an MoE. The same recipe worked here too: KL dropped from 0.175 to 0.066 after training, top-1 agreement reached 0.889, and task scores were the best of any pair I tried:

method SQuAD F1 HotpotQA F1 GSM8K
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B itself 0.918 0.747 0.922
Qwen3.5-4B prefill → transfer 0.906 (98.7%) 0.705 (94.5%) 0.838 (90.8%)
Qwen3.5-4B alone 0.897 0.720 0.855

But for this pair, transfer does not help much with speed. The MoE activates about 3B parameters per token, fewer than the dense 4B that would replace it in prefill. At 8k tokens the 35B-A3B prefills in 0.23 s and the 4B in 0.18 s. Once the maps and the DeltaNet fill are added, transfer is 0.88–1.03× the native speed: slower at every length except 2k. This is a feasibility result: the cache of a sparse model can be predicted from a dense one. For speed, you would pair a much larger MoE with a much smaller prefiller.

I also tried google/gemma-4-E4B → gemma-4-26B-A4B, and it is blocked by a library bug. In transformers 5.23, Gemma-4’s cached decoding path disagrees with its own full forward pass (KL 0.10 on a continuation even with the exact cache), so any transfer number would measure the bug, not the mapper. I stopped there and kept a small script that reproduces the mismatch.

Experiment 7: across model families and tokenizers

So far, we have transferred between models in the same family. Now we try two cross-family pairs: Qwen3-4B → Gemma3-12B and Gemma3-4B → Qwen3-14B.

These pairs introduce a new challenge. Qwen3 and Gemma3 use different tokenizers, so they can split the same text into different tokens. To build the larger model’s cache, we need to decide which small-model position supplies the information for each large-model token.

We align the tokens by character position. For each large-model token, we select the small-model token that contains its last character. We also make three changes to the mapper setup:

  • We add the large model’s token embedding as an input to the mapper. This only requires an embedding lookup.
  • We let the large model prefill the <bos> token and use its own keys and values for that attention sink.
  • We match source layers to target layers by their relative depth in each model.

The results are mixed:

Prefiller → answering model KL before training KL after training
Qwen3-4B → Gemma3-12B 0.373 0.181
Gemma3-4B → Qwen3-14B 0.873 0.135

The task scores compare each answering model using the transferred cache, using its own cache, and answering closed book. In the closed-book runs, we do not give the model the document or a document cache; the model still processes the question itself. We do not report a closed-book score for GSM8K.

Prefiller Answering model SQuAD F1 HotpotQA F1 GSM8K accuracy
Qwen3-4B, transferred cache Gemma3-12B 0.577 0.449 0.325
Gemma3-12B Gemma3-12B 0.806 0.646 0.917
None, closed book Gemma3-12B 0.233 0.266 –
Gemma3-4B, transferred cache Qwen3-14B 0.380 0.104 0.242
Qwen3-14B Qwen3-14B 0.789 0.655 0.945
None, closed book Qwen3-14B 0.276 0.270 –

In the Qwen → Gemma direction, the translated cache demonstrably carries the document: QA scores sit far above closed book. But Qwen3-4B on its own already scores 0.738 on this SQuAD setup, so the transfer is worse than not transferring at all. The Gemma → Qwen direction mostly fails: HotpotQA lands below closed book, which means the cache actively misleads the decoder. A curiosity: that direction reaches the better fidelity KL (0.135) and the worse task scores. Matching the next-token distribution on web text is not the same as preserving what a QA prompt needs.

Learnings:

  • Partial-layer transfer trades speed for accuracy. Letting the larger model compute its first layers can recover accuracy while still reducing prefill time.
  • Long contexts make a stronger case for transfer. The larger model using a transferred cache performs close to its own-cache baseline on LongBench v2.
  • Hybrid models need a different approach. Mapping DeltaNet inputs lets the larger model build its recurrent and convolution states, but that computation adds cost.
  • The prefiller’s compute matters for MoE models. A smaller dense model does not necessarily prefill faster than a larger sparse model.
  • Cross-family transfer needs more work. Token alignment carries information across model families, but the tested transfers do not beat the small model answering on its own.

item.title: I reverse engineered baseten’s 2000TPS inference engine
item.description:
Baseten posted that it had built an inference engine for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in Rust and CUDA, reaching around 2,060 tokens per second on eight B300 GPUs. It also reported prefilling a million tokens in roughly twelve seconds.

I wanted to understand how this was possible. Getting even 500 TPS is hard. I was curious to learn about the design choices and optimizations that lead to such insanely fast inference. Lucky for us, they open sourced the code.

The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash architecture

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is a causal encoder-decoder model. Its first 20 layers form the encoder, and the next 20 form the decoder. The decoder uses context supplied by the encoder, while a candidate pool feeds later sparse-indexing layers. The architecture also includes mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers and DSpark, a draft model used for speculative decoding.

The diagram from the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash paper shows how these components fit together:

The inference configuration gives the dimensions of these components:

Component Configuration
Target backbone 40 layers, hidden dimension 5,120
Routed MoE 384 experts per layer, 6 selected per token
Expert intermediate dimension 2,304
Attention 64 heads, head dimension 512
Sliding window 128 tokens
Main KV source layers 2, 8, 14, 20, using zero-based indices
Sparse attention selection Index top-k of 512
DSpark drafter 3 MTP layers, 128 experts, top-3 routing
Markov correction Rank 256
Vocabulary 129,280

The model description also identifies shared global KV, sparse indexing, bounded sliding-window replay and Engram conditional lookup memory as architectural features. These affect how much work the engine needs to do, particularly when processing a long prompt.

The model stores hundreds of billions of expert weights. How many does it use for one token?

Consider just the routed feed-forward experts. With hidden dimension and intermediate dimension , one expert’s three matrices (gate projection , up projection , and down projection ) contain

weights. The three matrices supply the two SwiGLU input projections and the output projection.

Across forty layers and 384 routed experts per layer, that becomes

routed-expert weights. But a single target token selects six experts per layer:

Those 8.49 billion weights cover only the routed experts. The model also uses shared experts, attention projections, output heads and other components. Engram adds a large lookup table, but each token accesses only selected entries.

Baseten’s README reports both the output rate and the average time for one step of the engine’s generation loop:

Configuration in the README Decode rate Average step time
4 × GB300, TP4 1,740 tokens/s 3.30 ms
8 × B300, TP8 2,060 tokens/s 2.71 ms

TP4 and TP8 mean that one model execution is distributed across four or eight GPUs using tensor parallelism. These are GPUs cooperating on one request, rather than four or eight independent copies each producing that rate.

B300 vs. GB300

Both use Blackwell Ultra GPUs. An HGX B300 server connects eight GPUs to x86 CPUs. A GB300 NVL72 rack connects 72 GPUs to NVIDIA Grace CPUs. Both use NVLink to connect their GPUs. Baseten’s “4 × GB300” result uses four GPUs from a GB300 system, not the entire rack. More on the system differences.

The decode example generates HTML for a Tetris game, with thinking disabled in the reproduction request. The README’s million-token prefill is a separate result. It does not establish that the Tetris decode rate was achieved with a million tokens already in context.

What does 2,060 tokens per second require? Dividing one second by the output rate gives an average time per emitted token:

How many output tokens does the engine get from each step? We can work that out from 0.485 ms per emitted token, calculated above, and 2.71 ms per step, reported by Baseten.

What is step time?

A decode step is one run of the engine’s generation loop. The code also calls this an iteration; both terms mean the same thing. I’ll use step throughout this post. Step time is how long one step takes. Baseten reports an average of 2.71 ms per step on eight B300 GPUs, excluding the initial prompt-processing phase (prefill). A step can produce more than one output token, so step time and time per token can differ.

What happens in one step? I followed the decode loop to capture_spec and found three main calls:

dspark_draft() → verify_prep(...) → spec_accept

The engine drafts tokens, checks them with the target model and commits the result. The reported 2,060 TPS and 2.71 ms per step imply

Each step takes an average of 2.71 ms, so the number of steps per second is

So the engine runs about 369 steps per second, producing around 5.6 tokens each. But what are those 5.6 tokens? To understand that, we need to look more closely at what happens during speculative decoding.

What does acceptance length count?

In ordinary decoding, the main model generates one token, then uses that token to generate the next one. Speculative decoding adds a smaller draft model that proposes several tokens ahead. The main model, also called the target model, then checks those proposals together.

The engine commits a prefix of the draft and one additional token. If the selected prefix ends before the draft does, that additional token replaces the next draft token. For example:

Draft:       A  B  C  D
Accepted:    A  B  C
Replacement:          X
Output:      A  B  C  X

The output has 3 accepted draft tokens plus 1 replacement. This illustrates the count, not the acceptance algorithm: Baseten uses a block sampler that selects a prefix using probabilities, as we will see below.

What if all four draft tokens are accepted? The target has also computed a distribution for the position after D, so the engine can sample one more token from it:

Draft:       A  B  C  D
Accepted:    A  B  C  D
Next token:              X
Output:      A  B  C  D  X

Here the step produces 4 accepted draft tokens plus 1 new token. If no draft tokens are accepted, the step still produces a replacement.

The request logger calls the average number of output tokens per step the average acceptance length:

An acceptance length of 5.6 tokens/step therefore means approximately 4.6 accepted draft tokens/step + 1 additional token/step.

The README gives 5.6 as a summary across both configurations. Dividing it by the reported step times gives about 2,066 TPS at 2.71 ms and 1,697 TPS at 3.30 ms, close to but not exactly the headline rates of 2,060 and 1,740 TPS. These reported summaries are approximate.

The tokens from a step can also arrive together when streamed. An average of 0.485 ms per token does not mean a token arrives every 0.485 ms.

How does the engine draft and verify a block in 2.71 ms? Let’s follow a request into the decode loop.

From a prompt to generated tokens

The server’s rank workers share a job. Before decoding, they check for a reusable prompt prefix, run prefill and initialize the speculative state. Each decode step then replays a captured GPU graph:

A CUDA graph records a sequence of GPU operations so the server can launch them together. Here, one replay runs a speculative step: draft tokens, verify them, and commit the result.

After each step, the server reads a snapshot of the GPU’s progress and streams any new tokens. It can launch another step while reading an earlier snapshot, so the diagram shows the flow of work rather than a strict timeline. The loop continues until the request finishes.

How does Baseten produce several tokens per step?

DeepSeek’s DSpark drafter proposes several tokens for the target to check together. This is faster only if drafting and verifying them takes less time than generating them one at a time.

Why can the target check several tokens at once?

During ordinary decoding, the model must sample one token before it knows the input for the next. With a draft, the proposed tokens are already available. The target can process their positions together under a causal mask, then decide which proposals to keep.

DeepSeek includes a model-native proposer called DSpark. In this implementation, target features are collected from layers 37, 38, and 39. The preparation path projects those features and constructs the drafter’s KV context. The three small draft transformer layers, called MTP layers in the code, compute draft features for a block containing the current anchor and noise-token positions.

On SM103, the Blackwell Ultra device profile, the configuration override sets the draft limit to six tokens. To verify all six, the target model receives the current token, called the anchor, followed by the six draft tokens. It processes those seven tokens together.

How does the engine draft six tokens without six draft-model passes?

The draft path runs the three MTP layers over the block together. But each proposed token still needs to account for the token sampled before it. Baseten handles that dependency in the Markov kernel: instead of rerunning all three draft layers for each position, it adds a smaller, rank-256 correction to that position’s precomputed logits. The correction and sampling still run sequentially, and they still touch the vocabulary; the saving is avoiding another full draft-model pass for every candidate.

How the Markov correction works

For a candidate token at draft position , the correction is

Here comes from the parallel draft computation, is the previous sampled token’s Markov embedding, and is the projection vector for vocabulary item .

The diagram shows one draft position and three vocabulary tokens. The same previous-token embedding is used for every candidate; each candidate has its own projection vector and base logit. The corrected logits determine the distribution used to sample the next draft token.

The implementation shards the vocabulary across TP ranks. Each rank evaluates its portion, combines candidate information across ranks, and agrees on the next token. For sampling it adds Gumbel noise to corrected logits and selects a maximum. Ignoring finite-precision effects, the Gumbel-max identity gives

This samples from the distribution using scores that each GPU can calculate locally and then reduce across ranks. The kernel also saves the draft logits and normalization statistics needed for verification.

There is another reuse opportunity in the code. The _ld kernel loads chunks of Markov weights into shared memory before the sequential loop and reuses them across draft positions; another kernel handles shapes that cannot use this variant. This reduces repeated loading inside the draft tail, but the source alone cannot tell us how many milliseconds it saves.

DSpark and the Markov head are model features, not inventions unique to Baseten. SGLang implements the same model-specific head. The question for the engine is how efficiently it executes and connects that model to verification.

Can the engine avoid verifying unpromising drafts?

Verifying six draft tokens means processing seven token positions through the target model. If the later drafts are unlikely to be accepted, the engine can verify fewer positions instead. Baseten’s draft tail uses the model’s confidence scores to choose that number. A shorter verification can finish sooner, but it also limits how many tokens the step can produce.

How the confidence threshold works

The kernel accumulates sigmoid confidence scores. In simplified notation,

When cumulative confidence falls below the configured threshold, the kernel can stop drafting and select a shorter verification body. The SM103 defaults use 0.3 for TP4 and 0.2 for TP8, with reduced thresholds for the final positions. These are profile choices, not universal optimal constants.

How does that choice reach the target without sending the confidence score back to the CPU? capture_spec_vadapt builds a CUDA graph with a verification branch for each supported length. The confidence kernel selects a branch on the GPU, so the CPU does not have to read the confidence score and launch a different sequence of kernels each time.

The graph builder creates the branches:

let sinks = g.sinks()?;
let bodies = g.add_switch(&sinks, h, blk as u32)?;

The CUDA drafter writes the branch selection:

cudaGraphSetConditional((cudaGraphConditionalHandle)p.hcond,
                        (unsigned)(L - 1));

Together, these lines let the GPU choose the verification branch within the captured graph. The host still launches each step. SGLang also has confidence-aware verification planning; this is a difference in the inspected execution paths, not evidence that confidence-based verification is exclusive to Baseten.

What happens to rejected drafts?

It would be tempting to explain acceptance as “compare each draft token to the target’s argmax and keep the matching prefix.” That would describe a greedy setting. This server fixes temperature and top-p at one, and its selected verification sampler uses block-wise acceptance.

The sampler setup sets block: 1. The SM103 variant includes the shared sample.cu code, so we can follow the acceptance logic there.

For orientation, ordinary token-wise speculative sampling accepts a proposal with probability and corrects rejection using a normalized positive residual . That example explains why draft probabilities are needed; it is not the complete rule used here.

Reading the actual block sampler

Let’s number the draft tokens . At position , let be the target distribution and the draft distribution. samp_stats stores the log ratio of their probabilities for the proposed token:

In samp_block, define

That is the source’s cumulative sum, running maximum, and expf(c - mx). The subtraction bounds by one. It is not the product of individually clipped acceptance probabilities.

For position , the kernel forms positive residual weights

Vocabulary shards contribute to the residual mass and to sampled token reductions. The acceptance tests for candidate block lengths use

The code ballots the passing tests and chooses the largest passing length. It does not count consecutive passing token comparisons from the beginning. At that length it selects the residual token when available, with the target draw as the fallback or full-block bonus.

These equations follow the implementation; they are not a proof of its floating-point, synchronization or random-number behavior. They do show that the sampler does more than compare each draft token to the target’s argmax.

Source: samp_stats and samp_block.

The final commit kernel writes the accepted draft tokens and the sampler’s extra token. It then updates the position, counters and next anchor on the GPU for the next step.

The counter updates make the rate calculation concrete:

state[0] = tok;
state[1] += 1;
state[2] += c;
state[3] += c + 1;

Here c is the number of accepted draft tokens. state[1] counts steps, while state[3] counts committed tokens: the accepted drafts plus one extra token.

Correctness and precision are separate questions here. A mathematically distribution-preserving sampler targets the probabilities computed by its numerical implementation. It does not make a quantized target identical to a higher-precision model. This engine can use an FP8 output head for verification at TP4, while the other profile differs. That deserves to be named when discussing output equivalence.

When does speculative decoding increase tokens per second?

The goal is not to draft the most tokens. It is to get the most committed tokens per second, including the time spent on drafting, target verification and sampling. A longer draft can improve that ratio if enough candidates are accepted; it can also make it worse by adding work that is thrown away.

The speculative decoding break-even point

Divide a speculative step’s elapsed time into non-overlapping contributions from drafting, verification, sampling/commit and gaps:

Its useful rate is

Against a matching plain one-token time , the symbolic speedup would be

We do not have a matching measured . Using Baseten’s reported 2.71 ms and roughly 5.6 tokens per step, the break-even plain-decoding time would be about ms per token. That is a threshold, not a measured baseline or speedup.

Longer drafts can also take more time to process and may select more experts. The best length depends on how many additional tokens are accepted.

How quickly can the GPU move and compute with the weights used in these steps? A roofline model gives us a way to start answering that question.

What can make block verification cheaper than separate passes?

The source points to a hardware opportunity. When several token vectors use the same weights, the GPU can reuse those weights within a matrix operation instead of loading them independently for each token. But whether that actually helps depends on memory traffic, GPU utilization and, for MoE layers, which experts the tokens choose.

A roofline model gives us a way to reason about the first two costs before following an actual Baseten kernel.

Roofline: compute versus memory traffic

Suppose we execute a matrix multiplication

Here is the number of token positions processed together. These can be positions from one speculative verification block, not necessarily separate user requests.

The useful multiplication performs approximately

Let be the bytes transferred between GPU memory and the chip, including weights, inputs, outputs and any scales or scratch data. Actual traffic also depends on caching and tiling. The arithmetic intensity is

For a large matrix and a few token positions, reading the weights dominates this simplified expression. Then

For FP8 weights this is approximately FLOPs/byte, before scale overhead. For FP4 plus one byte of scale per 32 weights,

One token position gives only about 3.76 FLOPs per weight-byte. Seven positions sharing that same matrix give about 26.35. That is better reuse, but it does not automatically fill the GPU’s tensor cores.

The roofline bound says

Equivalently, an idealized operation cannot finish sooner than

This is the framework developed in All About Rooflines. For this engine we also need collective latency, kernel dependencies, and shape constraints. A roofline is a lower-bound model, not a complete runtime simulator.

Why can memory bandwidth limit these projections?

NVIDIA’s October 2025 Blackwell Ultra datasheet, page 5 lists 8 TB/s HBM bandwidth for the GB300 configuration and 7.7 TB/s for HGX B300. Its FP8 figures are marked sparse; dividing by two gives dense peaks of 5 PFLOPS and 4.5 PFLOPS respectively. These are specification ceilings, not promised kernel throughput.

For the HGX B300 FP8 example, hardware balance is

An FP8 projection dominated by weight reads has an intensity near 2 for one token position and 14 for seven positions. Both are far below the crossover. Even with enormous compute capacity, the GPU can spend much of its time getting weights to the cores.

What does this look like for an actual projection in the engine? I followed one down to the GPU instructions.

How Baseten runs an attention projection on the GPU

Consider tg2_wqkv. It combines the query latent projection and the KV projection. The target configuration gives an input width of 5,120 and an output width of .

For seven token positions, the useful matrix multiplication is

It contains 9,175,040 weights and performs

With one-byte FP8 weight payload, its weight-only intensity is 14 FLOPs/byte. At 7.7 TB/s, reading that payload alone takes an ideal 1.19 microseconds; at 4.5 PFLOPS, its useful arithmetic takes an ideal 0.029 microseconds. Neither is a prediction of kernel duration. The disparity explains why memory delivery, tile shape, launch/dependency costs and the fused surrounding work deserve more attention than the headline FLOPS.

The weight loader builds this fused projection without splitting its output channels by rank. Other projections are split across heads, groups or intermediate dimensions, so we cannot divide every operation by the number of GPUs.

The engine chooses how to split the operation for the matrix shape and GPU. The kernel uses tensor-map descriptors for asynchronous transfers. At the hardware level, tc.cuh stages tiles in shared memory and uses Blackwell tensor memory for the tensor-core path. Barriers coordinate transfers and computation, allowing them to overlap when dependencies permit.

The MMA wrapper’s assembly string identifies the hardware operation directly:

tcgen05.mma.cta_group::1.kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale

How fusion can reduce memory transfers and kernel launches

The GEMV interfaces have options for normalization, quantized output, RoPE, split outputs and sampling records. In attention, the engine can combine query projection with normalization, RoPE and KV processing. The output projection can also prepare a packed input for the next operation and, on supported paths, write into the collective’s mailbox.

Suppose an unfused pipeline materializes a BF16 intermediate and the next stage rereads it. Removing one complete write/read pair saves

For , that saves 143,360 bytes. Fusion can also remove a kernel launch or a wait between operations. Those savings matter when many small operations run one after another.

Fusion has costs too. Larger kernels can need more registers and shared memory, restrict co-residency, or become specialized to shapes that fit their synchronization scheme. The source contains shared-memory budgets, supported-shape tests and fallback paths for precisely this kind of constraint. A fused kernel is not automatically better at every size.

The projection above uses the same weights for every token position. Does that still hold inside the model’s mixture-of-experts layers?

Why MoE tokens do not always share expert weights

For a dense projection, seven token vectors all multiply the same weight matrix. An MoE layer chooses experts separately for each token. Seven tokens can select seven different sets of matrices.

Let be the selected experts per token, the number of token positions, and the number of tokens assigned to expert . If distinct experts are touched, then

Under an idealized one-fetch-per-touched-expert assumption, weight traffic is

For seven token positions there are two useful extremes:

Routing across seven tokens Distinct experts Useful FLOPs per logical weight-byte
All tokens choose the same six 6 26.35
All selections are disjoint 42 3.76
A toy model of expert reuse

For a hypothetical independent uniform router, the probability an expert is never selected is . Therefore,

This gives about 3.94 FLOPs per byte when dividing expected work by expected weight traffic. Actual routes can be correlated, and a kernel can fetch weights more than once.

The target can verify several token positions together, but those positions may need different experts. That limits how much expert-weight traffic they can share. Other work, such as dense projections, scheduling and communication, can still be shared across the verification block.

Estimating the time to read expert weights from GPU memory

The logical routed-expert bytes associated with one target token across forty layers are

That is about 4.51 GB, including the logical FP4 scale overhead but excluding layout padding, activations, shared experts, attention, and everything else.

If those weights are read from HBM once, perfectly balanced across four GB300 GPUs at 8 TB/s each, the ideal component floor is

For eight HGX B300 GPUs at 7.7 TB/s each, it is approximately 0.073 ms. For a seven-token verification block, the uniform-router model multiplies the single-token weight traffic by , giving about 0.489 ms for that routed-weight component on TP8.

This estimate assumes the weights come from HBM, work is perfectly balanced, and each needed expert is fetched once. Caching could reduce the HBM reads; layout and scheduling could increase them. We have also left out the drafter, attention, other matrices, sampling and synchronization.

The estimate is small enough that 2.71 ms per step is plausible. It does not predict the full step time: we would need to account for the rest of the work and its dependencies.

How does Baseten execute the MoE layers?

This line in sgl_init is unusually direct:

"sgl moe: {} layers on SGLang's low-batch MoE chain"

That is the source’s description of its own path. The loader enables SGL packing for the supported target shapes, and sgl_moe_on enables the path for the SM103 TP4 and TP8 profiles. The target uses it at both sizes; the drafter’s SGL path has an additional TP8 gate.

The engine runs without the SGLang runtime, but its code explicitly identifies this MoE chain with SGLang. The README also says the agents optimizing its kernels could read SGLang and FlashInfer. I haven’t traced the exact history of each kernel, so I won’t claim which lines came from where.

The active call chain is

weights.rs selects SGL layout
  → ffn_sgl builds routing/GEMM arguments
    → sgl_moe_launch
      → router
      → GEMM1: input projections and activation
      → GEMM2: output projection
    → communication/finalization boundary

The router picks experts and prepares their inputs, weights and work records. GEMM1 runs the two input projections, applies clamped SwiGLU and quantizes the result. GEMM2 uses that result to produce the expert outputs. The chain also handles the shared expert. The next communication stage can then combine the expert outputs using the routing weights, without a separate finalization pass first.

These kernels are designed to work together. The router prepares the layout that the GEMMs need, and the collective can consume their output directly.

How does Baseten’s MoE path compare with basic SGLang?

The key finding is more specific than “Baseten has a fast MoE kernel and SGLang does not.” At the pinned SGLang revision, the specialized CUDA MXFP4 decode MoE switch defaults to false. When enabled, its dispatch checks also require a supported GPU, expert shape, activation and precision. On eligible paths it uses a routing kernel followed by a persistent FC1/FC2 kernel; otherwise that conditional path is not selected. The exact fallback depends on the chosen backend and layer.

For Baseten’s supported SM103 TP4/TP8 target profiles, the loader and dispatch select its SGL-labeled low-batch MoE chain. Its router prepares records for the expert GEMMs, and its communication path can consume the expert outputs for finalization. This gives Baseten a concrete integration choice: the low-token-count expert path and the next communication boundary are designed together for this model and these shapes. It does not prove the SGLang kernel is absent, that the implementations are identical, or how much faster either path is.

The broader comparison changes if SGLang is configured for the same job. Its speculative algorithm field defaults to None, while Baseten’s decode path uses DSpark. SGLang also supports DSpark when configured, so an apples-to-apples investigation must test both a basic setup and one with DSpark and eligible low-batch MoE enabled. Match model, GPU count, precision, prompt, output length and sampling too. No matched timings are available here, so the code identifies differences in execution, not a measured TPS gap.

How splitting experts across GPUs affects memory usage

At TP4, each expert’s intermediate dimension is per GPU; at TP8 it is . Padding means that halving the useful channels does not halve packed storage.

Expert packing at TP4 and TP8

The packing functions align the W13 side to 128 channels and the W2 input-channel payload to 64. We can calculate the allocated packed bytes for one expert’s two buffers from the actual formulas:

Configuration Logical channels per rank W13 padded channels W2 payload channels Packed bytes per rank
TP4 576 640 576 5,058,560
TP8 288 384 320 2,969,600

The unpadded FP4-plus-scale expert is 18,800,640 bytes globally. Multiplying the packed buffers by the rank count gives about 20.23 MB at TP4 and 23.76 MB at TP8: approximately 7.6% and 26.4% storage overhead respectively.

These are allocated bytes, not necessarily bytes read for every token.

The decoder kernels explicitly support a small range of token counts. moe_rows_ok rejects unsupported verification shapes on the tensor-core paths, in part to prevent silently switching to different numerics. The code is not trying to make one kernel equally good for one token and a large prefill batch.

The repository also contains tmoe_fused and separate prefill kernels. The loader and dispatch branches tell us which path is selected for a given configuration.

Each GPU computes only part of the work. Those results also need to be combined, so the next question is how much communication sits between the layers.

How GPUs exchange results between model layers

Tensor parallelism reduces some local matrix work, but ranks must combine partial results. Repeating that combination at attention and feed-forward boundaries creates dependencies between layers.

A useful communication model is

Here is the number of latency-bearing phases, is the phase latency, and is traffic on the bottleneck link or resource. The payload’s logical size alone does not determine : the algorithm may replicate, reduce or exchange it in several stages.

In comm_ex, the selected path can use NVLink multicast buffers, profile-specific attention/FFN kernels, and specialized producer-push or Lamport-related communication variants. Its CUDA implementations combine arrival detection, reduction, and surrounding computation. This avoids treating communication as an isolated library call between separately materialized tensors.

Combining GPU communication with layer operations

The model uses mHC residual mixing, with four residual streams in its configuration. Beyond summing TP partials, a boundary may need to combine routed and shared expert outputs, apply residual mixing, and prepare the next sublayer’s input.

The FFN path passes expert output buffers, routing/permutation records, shared output and mHC state to the communication path. An eligible attention output projection can publish into the receive mailbox directly. The corresponding consumer checks the producer’s completion state before consuming the payload.

These are logical dependencies, not necessarily separate launches. By writing data in a form the collective can consume, the producer can avoid copies and waits.

The griddepcontrol helpers implement programmatic dependent launch, or PDL. A producer can make a dependent kernel eligible before it has completely finished, while the dependent kernel waits at the point required by the protocol. Work such as loading weights can then overlap with remaining producer work. This does not authorize reading unfinished output; correctness still depends on the explicit waits and publication conditions.

Side streams serve a related purpose. Indexer/compressor work, mHC calculations and Engram preparation can start before their results are first needed. The main path joins them at their consumers. Whether this saves time depends on available SM and memory resources. If both kernels need a resource that is already saturated, running them on separate streams will not make the work disappear.

Why eight GPUs do not necessarily double decode speed

The headline ratio is

It is not a clean strong-scaling experiment: the platform labels, thresholds, draft MoE path, output-head choice and other profile decisions differ. But the code gives good reasons not to expect a factor of two. Some projections and state are replicated; communication remains; small local dimensions pad; and the serial draft/verification chain still exists.

An overall step has both resource constraints and a critical path. We can lower-bound it using compute and traffic, but the longest chain of dependent operations also matters:

A single roofline for all the model’s FLOPs and bytes would miss the order in which operations depend on each other. Adding every kernel duration is not enough either, because some kernels overlap. We need to consider both the dependencies and the resources the kernels share.

That explains the path for generating output. The announcement also makes a separate claim about processing long prompts, so let’s follow the prefill path next.

How the engine processes a million-token prompt

The separate prefill result is one of the most interesting parts of the repository. It is easy to read it as “the kernels process a million tokens through forty layers in twelve seconds.” The code does something more model-specific.

In prefill_inner, dec0 is half the target layer count. The function checks the architecture’s window and source-layer invariants, then streams prompt chunks through the first twenty layers. It constructs the layer-20 source KV and saves the encoder’s recent output in a tail buffer.

Next, replay_decoder restores the encoder outputs for the most recent 128 tokens and executes the remaining twenty layers over those token positions, using the available source KV.

An abridged reconstruction of the control flow is:

// Schematic: error handling, cache restoration and metadata omitted.
for chunk in prompt_chunks {
    forward_impl(chunk, 0, 20, /* embed */ true, /* head */ false);
    stream_kv_source(20, chunk);
    stash_tail(chunk);
}
replay_decoder(last_128_outputs, 20, 40);

Why can it omit decoder execution for older prompt tokens? In a conventional Transformer, each layer builds global KV from its own preceding hidden states. Old hidden states can be required to construct later layers’ attention state. Here the decoder’s global KV is sourced from the encoder side. That removes one dependency, but leaves the decoder’s local sliding-window state to reconstruct.

The paper’s Section 3.2.2 makes an important distinction: replaying only the last window approximates that local state. Dependencies accumulate across decoder layers, so exact reconstruction would need a longer replay. The bounded version truncates local attention at the replay boundary. DeepSeek reports little quality degradation in its evaluations, but the result is not mathematically identical to a full decoder forward pass. Source: SWA Bounded Replay.

The source-sharing structure and local-window rules are essential to this tradeoff. The engine explicitly checks them. An unrelated decoder-only model would not inherit the same justification for skipping its decoder work.

We can count token positions processed by each layer as a simple work proxy. A conventional full-layer schedule over prompt tokens would perform layer-token evaluations. This schedule has

backbone layer-token evaluations, plus source-KV construction and other work. At :

The ratio is about 0.500064. That is nearly half the layer-token evaluations. It is not proof of an exact twofold reduction in FLOPs or time: different layers do different attention/indexing work, and replay has its own overhead.

This gives us an explanation that faster matmuls alone would miss: the engine uses a shorter prefill schedule, accepting approximate local state. The opportunity comes partly from the model design; SGLang also has decoder-tail replay machinery.

How sparse attention selects past context

The target combines a local window with selected compressed global KV. The indexer scores candidates, and later decoder layers can reuse a candidate pool. Sparse attention reduces the entries read by attention, but selecting them still requires computation and cache management.

How saved conversation caches differ from GPU memory allocation

The server can retain conversation state and transfer it between replicas, avoiding recomputation of a reusable prefix. The snapshot encoder stores compact source state and a bounded tail; the GPU allocator reserves separate buffers for active inference. A small saved snapshot therefore does not imply equally small live GPU memory use. Whether restoring it is faster than recomputation depends on the prefix, cache location and network.

Which optimizations also exist in SGLang and vLLM?

The earlier MoE comparison shows that a basic SGLang configuration and Baseten do not necessarily select the same execution path. SGLang also implements DSpark, confidence-aware verification, capturable sampling and acceptance, and decoder-tail replay. Their availability does not mean they are all enabled in a given run.

vLLM has an opt-in DeepSeek-V4.1 latency_specialized backend with small-token-count kernels, fused boundaries and vocabulary-sharded Markov sampling. It has specific hardware and configuration requirements; its default auto setting uses the stock path. The B300 TP4 recipe describes a specialized deployment.

These implementations show that the underlying techniques are not exclusive to Baseten. The source reveals different configurations and integration choices, but without matched measurements it does not establish a TPS ranking.

Tradeoffs behind the speed

Baseten specializes the engine to this model, a small range of token counts and Blackwell GPU profiles. That enables tailored layouts, kernels and graph branches, but a different model or shape may need different paths. The API also restricts temperature and top-p to one.

The worker loop serves one shared generation job at a time. The reported decode rate therefore does not tell us aggregate throughput, queueing latency or cost per token under concurrent load. Speculation also depends on draft acceptance: candidates that are not committed still consume GPU time.

Precision and prefill matter too. The engine uses FP4, FP8 and higher-precision operations in different places, with output-head choices that vary by profile. The bounded prefill replay reconstructs local state approximately. Neither choice should be treated as identical to every possible reference configuration.

How much does the 2,060 TPS result tell us?

The source shows how the result can come from several mechanisms working together: DeepSeek’s sparse architecture and DSpark drafter, low-precision weights, GPU-side verification, kernels designed for small token counts, and fused communication. The reported 2,060 TPS corresponds to about 5.6 output tokens per 2.71 ms step.

This is substantial specialization, and the code itself identifies one active MoE chain with SGLang. It does not establish how much faster Baseten is than a matched SGLang or vLLM deployment, or how the result generalizes to other prompts and loads. Those questions need measurements under the same conditions.

Source revisions and arithmetic

This article studies the following snapshots, rather than assuming that a moving main branch always behaves the same way:

Source Revision
Baseten DeepSeek Ultrafast 76766a97308bfd1658fb055e835d0f92de737dc3
SGLang a56dbcf181cfb7f395c340a093ec5a0bca22cae5
vLLM, targeted source inspection 9bc16ae6a34b1e0fe260e8d12b98568478bf38c3
DeepSeek model repository 314113f8a7dadb388215396ba5fbee2c610a04d6

The article’s source links are pinned to those revisions. The vLLM comparison is targeted; it is not an audit of every backend or its entire scheduler. No independent GPU timing or numerical-equivalence result is claimed here.

The calculation and figure script reproduces the analytical examples and their plots with Python, NumPy and Matplotlib. All byte counts use decimal GB/TB unless stated otherwise. Logical traffic, allocated packed storage and measured hardware transfers are kept separate.

item.title: Keeping 32 agents warm on one GPU
item.description:
When you chat with a language model, the reply shows up one word at a time (in this post, “word” and “token” mean the same thing; tokens get a proper definition in a moment). That is not a stylistic choice. The model really does work that way: it writes one word, then looks at everything so far (your whole conversation, plus its reply up to that point) and writes the next one.

“Looks at everything so far” sounds expensive. It would be, if the model reread the whole conversation from scratch for every word. It does not. As it reads, it keeps notes on every word it has already seen, and for each new word it only has to consult those notes.

Those notes are called the KV cache. K and V stand for “keys” and “values”, and they work like the keys and values of a dictionary:

  • a key is a label. You match against it to decide whether this entry is the one you want.
  • a value is the content. It is what you take away once you have picked the entry.

Every word the model reads gets one of each. Its key describes what the word is about, and its value is the information the word passes on to whoever picks it. Both are nothing more exotic than lists of numbers (vectors). The model is a stack of layers (a transformer), and every layer computes its own key and value for every word.

A new word uses them to look back. Say the model has written “the cat” and is now working on “sat”. Each layer takes what “sat” is looking for (its query), compares it against the keys of “the” and “cat”, and finds that “cat” matches best. It then pulls in mostly the value of “cat”, and a little of “the”. Unlike a real dictionary, the lookup is soft: every entry contributes, weighted by how well its key matches. This looking back is called attention.

The keys and values of “the” and “cat” are the same no matter what comes after them. So the model can keep them and reuse them for every later word. If it does not keep them, it has to recompute them, and that means running “the” and “cat” through every layer of the model again, for every new word.

How much does keeping them save? I measured it. I gave a model (Qwen3-8B) a long conversation, about 64,000 words, on the GPU I used for this post. With its notes, the model wrote each new word in 18 milliseconds. Without them, rereading the conversation took 6.2 seconds per word. That is 346 times slower.

The notes have a price, though. For that one conversation they take up 9.7 GB of the GPU’s memory, more than half the size of the model itself. That memory is scarce, because a GPU serving many conversations has to hold everyone’s notes at once. The notes also have to be read, all of them, for every new word. And if they are ever thrown away to make room for someone else, rebuilding them costs those 6.2 seconds again.

This is a long post, and it grows one chapter at a time. Chapter 0 builds the KV cache from scratch: what a model does with a word, what keys and values are, why they can be kept, and what keeping them costs, measured on a real GPU. Then it puts the cache under the hardest load I know, coding agents, and sets a target: serve 32 of them on one GPU. Every chapter after that takes one way this target fails and works on it.

What every number in this post ran on
  • GPU. One NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, 96 GB of memory.
  • Engine. SGLang 0.5.23 (torch 2.14.1, CUDA 13.0, FlashInfer 0.7.2), an open-source inference server: the program that holds the model in GPU memory, accepts requests, batches them and manages the cache. It may use 85% of GPU memory for weights and caches.
  • Model. Qwen3-8B. It was trained for 32K-token conversations; I run it at 131,072 tokens using YaRN, a standard trick that stretches the model’s sense of position by a factor of 4.
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --json-model-override-args '{"rope_scaling":{"rope_type":"yarn","factor":4.0,"original_max_position_embeddings":32768},"max_position_embeddings":131072}' \
  --context-length 131072 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 --enable-metrics

Every measurement below uses this server with at most one flag changed; each callout says which.

Chapter 0: What a KV cache is, and what it costs

How a language model writes

A language model reads and writes tokens, which are chunks of text, usually a word or part of one. Qwen’s tokenizer splits “def flush_cache():” into 4 of them: def, flush, _cache, ():. The model’s whole job is to look at a sequence of tokens and output, for every token in its vocabulary, a probability that it comes next.

To write a reply, you run that in a loop:

  1. Feed in the conversation so far.
  2. Pick the next token from the probabilities.
  3. Append it to the conversation.
  4. Go back to 1.

This is autoregressive generation. A 500-token reply is 500 trips around the loop, and each trip produces exactly one token. Hold on to that loop; the KV cache exists because of it.

Inside a transformer

The model is a big function with billions of numbers inside it, called parameters or weights. Qwen3-8B has about 8 billion, and I host it in BF16. At 2 bytes each that is 16 GB, and all of it has to sit in GPU memory, because every token passes through all of it.

Those weights are arranged as a transformer:

  1. An embedding table turns each token into a list of 4,096 numbers, a vector. Think of it as the token’s running notes.
  2. A stack of 36 identical layers each reads those notes and adds to them. Each layer has two parts:
    • attention, the only place where a token reads other tokens’ notes, and
    • an MLP, which processes each token’s notes on its own.
  3. An output layer turns the last token’s final notes into next-token probabilities.

Here is one layer, from the point of view of the newest token :

The token’s vector is normalized (RMSNorm just rescales it), then multiplied by three weight matrices, , and . That gives three new vectors: a query , a key and a value . Attention uses them to pull in information from earlier tokens, mixes the result back into the token’s vector, and the MLP processes it further.

How big are these pieces? The shapes in Figure 1 are enough to count every weight in a layer:

The count matches the checkpoint to within the tiny normalization weights, so the picture is right. And look at where the weights are: the key and value projections are only 4% of each layer.

Attention, and what K and V depend on (the precise version)

This is the intro’s soft dictionary lookup, written out precisely for one layer. Write for token ’s vector as it enters layer . The query, key and value are three projections of it (the , , boxes in Figure 1):

RoPE (rotary position embedding) is how the model knows where tokens are. It rotates pairs of numbers inside the query and the key by an angle proportional to the token’s position, so their dot product ends up depending on how far apart the two tokens are.

Token ’s output scores its query against the key of every token up to and including itself, turns the scores into weights that sum to 1 with a softmax, and takes the weighted average of the values:

is the vector length, and dividing by keeps the scores in a sane range. Qwen3-8B does this with 32 heads per layer, each with its own query of length , each free to look for something different. And a token only ever looks backwards, . This is causal attention.

Because attention is causal, token ’s key and value are built only from tokens . Three things follow:

  • They never change once computed, so they can be cached.
  • They are expensive to rebuild: and are only 4% of a layer, but at layer 20 needs token to pass through layers 1–19 first.
  • They are only valid behind the exact same prefix, since they depend on every earlier token and, through RoPE, on position.

Just as important is what does not need keeping. The query is used once, by its own token. The MLP’s intermediate numbers are thrown away. Even itself can go, since its only lasting purpose was producing and .

Why there is a cache at all

A token’s key and value depend only on the tokens up to it, so once computed they never change. When the model writes token 1,001, the keys and values of tokens 1 to 1,000 are exactly the ones it computed on the previous trip. So there are two ways to run the loop:

  1. Recompute. Run the whole conversation through the model again for every new token.
  2. Store. Keep every key and value from every head of every layer. For each new token, compute only its query, key and value, and read the old keys and values from memory.

Six tokens: 21 computations against 6. The gap grows quadratically, so let us count it properly.

A FLOP is one floating-point operation, a multiply or an add. Pushing one token through a weight matrix with numbers in it costs FLOPs: one multiply and one add per weight. So one token through the whole model costs about FLOPs, and generating tokens after an -token prompt costs

How much more work is recomputing? Divide the two:

For a 64K-token conversation () and a 500-token reply (), that is : recomputing does about 65,786× more work than storing. And that counts only the matmuls; attention makes recomputing worse still. The memory in option 2 is the KV cache, named after what it holds.

So the KV cache trades compute for memory: it stores what it would otherwise recompute. There is a third side to the trade. Stored numbers are only useful once they are moved from memory to the GPU’s math units, so the cache also spends communication: bytes moved per second. These three sides, compute, memory and communication, are the trade-off this whole post keeps coming back to.

The trade-off: compute, memory and communication

Memory. For every token, the cache stores one key vector and one value vector per key/value head, in every attention layer. With attention layers, key/value heads of dimension , and bytes per number,

The factor of 2 counts keys and values. For Qwen3-8B, , and . Note that is 8, not the 32 query heads of Figure 1: and produce only 8 heads’ worth of keys and values, and each group of 4 query heads shares one of them. This is grouped-query attention (GQA; Ainslie et al., 2023). In BF16 (),

Figure 3 compares this with the size of the model itself.

GQA is one way of making this trade-off. Sharing each key/value head among query heads divides the cache by 4, which reduces both the memory a token occupies and the bytes every decode step must read. It leaves the cost of recomputation almost unchanged: and account for only 4% of a layer’s weights, and rebuilding a token’s keys and values still requires running it through every layer. The cost is some model quality, since four query heads now attend over the same keys. With GQA, one conversation’s cache exceeds the model’s weights at 111K tokens; without it, at 28K, and a single 120K-token conversation would not fit on this GPU.

How much fits. SGLang loads the weights, reserves working memory for in-flight computation, and allocates the rest of its 85% budget as a single cache pool. We therefore expect a pool of 70.9 GB. The server’s startup log reports what it actually allocated:

Load weight end. elapsed=0.92 s, type=Qwen3ForCausalLM, avail mem=78.95 GB, mem usage=15.32 GB.
KV Cache is allocated. dtype: torch.bfloat16, #tokens: 471816, K size: 32.40 GB, V size: 32.40 GB
max_total_num_tokens=471816, chunked_prefill_size=8192, max_prefill_tokens=16384, max_running_requests=2048, context_len=131072, available_gpu_mem=10.51 GB

The pool holds 471,816 tokens (69.6 GB), 2% below the estimate; the difference is working buffers. This is the memory budget of the whole server: 472K tokens of cache shared by every conversation, or 7.2 conversations of 64K tokens.
