In the synthetic workload, each agent starts either with the shared system prompt or with a private prompt of the same length, which the tree has to store separately. If a fraction of the agents share it, the shared copy is stored once and every other agent carries its own:

I ran 24 agents on Qwen3-8B with = 0, ½ and 1.

Sharing the system prompt halves what each agent holds, and that roughly doubles the agents that fit, from 6.9 to 13.2. 24 agents is past the cliff in every row, so the hit rate is Chapter 2’s floor: the only thing that survives is the shared prompt. With nobody sharing, there is no floor, and the hit rate is zero. With everybody sharing it is 59%, and the median wait drops from 186 s to 42 s.

A system prompt is free compression of the cache, on one condition: every agent has to send exactly the same one, byte for byte. That is Chapter 1’s lesson again, at the scale of the whole server instead of one session.

What sharing leaks

Now let the agents belong to different customers. R6 says one customer must learn nothing about another, and a shared cache is a side channel. A prompt someone else already sent skips its prefill, so it comes back faster, and the speed is visible to whoever sent it second.

How much faster is a matter of arithmetic. Prefilling 4,096 tokens on Qwen3-8B costs about 166 ms on the napkin, and a full hit costs one step, about 18 ms. I measured it as an attack. Customer A either sends a 4,096-token prompt or does not, at random. Then customer B sends the same prompt and times its first token. B wins if it can tell which happened. Over 400 trials:

With a shared cache the answer is not subtle. A hit returns in 16 ms and a miss in 179 ms, so one threshold is right every time. B does not even need a stopwatch: the response’s cached_tokens field says 4,095 when A was there.

The fix is to salt the cache per customer: mix a per-customer key into the tree, so that two requests only share a prefix if they share the key too.

SGLang’s /generate takes such a key as extra_key. With one per customer, B waits the same 182 ms either way, and its guess is right 53% of the time: a coin flip.

Salting costs one copy of the system prompt per customer. With customers on the GPU:

With a handful of customers per GPU, that costs a few agents, much less than sharing nothing. It is a cost to choose on purpose: put the salt on the customer, not on the user or the session. Salt per session and every agent carries its own copy, which is the 0% row of the earlier table.

Command: probing a shared cache, and salting it 
import random, time, requests
URL = "http://localhost:30000"

def first_token(ids, key=None):
    body = {"input_ids": ids, "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 1}} | ({"extra_key": key} if key else {})
    t = time.perf_counter()
    r = requests.post(URL + "/generate", json=body).json()
    return time.perf_counter() - t, r["meta_info"]["cached_tokens"]

for salt in (False, True):
    right = 0
    for i in range(400):
        requests.post(URL + "/flush_cache")
        secret = [random.randrange(1000, 150_000) for _ in range(4096)]
        present = i % 2 == 0
        if present:
            first_token(secret, "customer-a" if salt else None)       # A sends it, or not
        wait, cached = first_token(secret, "customer-b" if salt else None)
        right += (wait < 0.08) == present                             # B guesses from the wait alone
    print("salted" if salt else "shared", right / 400)

Where this leaves me

Sharing is the one way to make a cache smaller without approximating anything, and on agent traffic there is exactly one thing to share: the prefix. Inside a session, the trace has no out-of-order repeats to recover. Across agents, the system prompt halves what each one holds, and keeping customers apart costs one copy of it per customer.

That still leaves each agent with its own 33K-token conversation, stored in 16-bit numbers. The next factor to attack is the bits.

Chapter 5: Fewer bits

Chapter 0 tried smaller numbers first and found they buy room: an FP8 cache holds twice the tokens, NVFP4 about 3.4 times. It left R4, quality, for later. Sharing has given all it can, so now R4 has to be measured.

How a number loses bits

A floating-point number is stored as a sign, an exponent and a mantissa: . The exponent sets the scale, and the mantissa sets the precision within that scale. BF16 has 8 exponent bits and 7 mantissa bits. The FP8 format SGLang uses, E4M3, has 4 and 3. That leaves two problems.

  • Precision. With 3 mantissa bits, neighbouring numbers are 1/8 apart in relative terms, so rounding moves a number by up to 1/16 of itself: about 6%.
  • Range. With 4 exponent bits, the largest E4M3 number is 448 and the smallest normal one is . Anything smaller loses precision fast, and anything larger does not fit.

To fit the range, numbers are divided by a scale before rounding and multiplied back after:

A good puts the largest number near the top of the range. One large number then forces a large , and every small number around it is pushed down toward the bottom of the range, where precision runs out. NVFP4 (E2M1) can only represent 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6. It gets away with it by giving every block of 16 numbers its own scale, but within a block, one outlier sets the scale for the other 15.

So whether a cache survives fewer bits depends on how its numbers are spread out. That is something to measure.

How much change is “no measurable change”?

R4 says no measurable change, and that needs a yardstick. The model’s output is not perfectly repeatable even in BF16. GPU kernels add numbers in an order that depends on the batch, and floating-point addition is not associative: once rounding is involved. So I measured BF16 against itself first.

The measurement, Q1, compares the next-token probabilities two configurations give. Take 200 windows of real code (SGLang’s own source) between 1K and 128K tokens. Put each window in the cache, then feed the next 512 tokens of the file and record the model’s top-20 next-token probabilities at every one of them. At each position, the distance between the reference distribution and the test distribution is the KL divergence:

0 means identical. I only have the top 20 tokens of each, so I compute it over those tokens plus one bucket for everything else, which gives a lower bound on the full KL.

For the floor, both configurations are the same BF16 server, once with requests one at a time and once 16 at a time:

Even BF16 picks a different top token about once in a hundred positions when only the batch changes, and greedy generation from the same prompt drifts apart after a hundred-odd tokens. So “no measurable change” cannot mean zero. I set R4’s threshold at five times this floor: an approximation passes if it moves the model no further than five batch changes would.

A small KL is not the same as a working agent, so I added a second check, Q2, for the task an agent actually does with a long context: find something it read earlier. Each of 100 synthetic sessions hides a fact (a token, a path, a config value) in a tool result, pads the conversation with more tool results until the fact is 4K to 100K tokens back, and then asks for it.

What the smaller numbers cost

Retrieval does not notice. Every format finds the same facts as BF16 to within a couple out of 100, which is the noise of a 100-question test. At these depths, a 4-bit cache still knows where everything is.

The probabilities do notice, and the two models react very differently. On Qwen3-8B, FP8 moves the model 2.0 times as far as R4 allows, and NVFP4 9 times. The damage grows with context: the more cached tokens a step reads, the more rounding error it adds up. Qwen3.5 passes with FP8 and misses by 19% with NVFP4, with no growth with context. That is the hybrid design again. Only 8 of Qwen3.5’s layers keep a cache, so only those 8 read rounded numbers. The cache format does not touch the DeltaNet states.

Keys or values?

Qwen3-8B fails even at FP8, so it is worth knowing where the error comes from. SGLang rounds keys and values together, so this one ran offline in plain PyTorch on Qwen3-8B: 50 windows of 8K tokens of code, with the keys, the values or both rounded to FP8 or NVFP4 before attention reads them, and the same KL against unrounded BF16. I tried two scales: , which is what SGLang uses when it has no calibration, and one calibrated per layer from the largest number seen on 8 other windows.

It is the keys. Rounding only the values costs almost nothing in either format, and rounding only the keys costs nearly everything that rounding both does. My first guess was outliers, and the calibration pass recorded the range of both:

The guess is half right. In the first layers, keys do carry numbers hundreds of times bigger than the values: 234 against 0.5 in layer 0. But from layer 28 on, the largest values are bigger than the largest keys, and rounding values still costs almost nothing. So range is not what separates them. Where the error goes is.

An error in a key hurts more than the same error in a value. A key enters attention through a dot product with every query, and the result goes into an exponent:

So a rounding error in multiplies the attention weight, for every query that looks at it. A rounding error in only adds a little noise to one term of an average, and averages forgive noise.

Calibrated scales help, but only by 22% for FP8. Applied to the served measurement, that would take Qwen3-8B’s FP8 from 7.4e-03 to about 5.7e-03, still above R4’s 3.6e-03. So I did not rerun the served test with calibrated scales.

Nor is there one bad layer that could stay in BF16. Rounding a single layer’s keys to NVFP4, the worst layer costs only 1.6× the median layer. The error is spread across the model.

The cheap option this points at is mixed formats, with values in 4 bits and keys in 8. SGLang 0.5.23 has one --kv-cache-dtype for both, so I could not serve it.

Where the cliff moves

Quality aside, does the room show up as agents? On the napkin, each format changes only the bytes-per-token term, so the cliff should move with the pool. I reran Chapter 2’s synthetic sweep in each format.

The napkin holds again. Each halving of the bytes moves the cliff out by about the factor the pool grew. But the points before the cliff do not pass the other requirements: the p90 wait is past R2 everywhere, and each user’s speed falls as more agents decode together, because every step still reads every cached token, only in fewer bytes.

The step does get cheaper per token, and by about what Chapter 0’s decode formula says, with the bytes per token halved or quartered:

NVFP4 comes in a little slower than its bytes say, probably the cost of unpacking 4-bit numbers and their scales. With one request it hardly matters, because the step is mostly reading the weights.

Qwen3.5: the other pool runs out

Qwen3.5 did not follow the napkin. Its token pool doubles with FP8 and nearly triples with NVFP4, but its cliff stayed where it was:

The first three rows are Chapter 2’s state pool again. Every run in this chapter used the 256 slots Chapter 2 chose, and Qwen3.5 has two pools with two limits. With requests running and agents parked:

The first says how many can run: at most 51 with 256 slots. The second says the two pools share one budget, so every slot costs as much memory as cached tokens. At 64 agents with NVFP4, 50 were running and 7 waiting, with the token pool only 80% full. Shrinking the tokens made more room in the pool that was not running out.

So the split has to move again. 256 slots were right when tokens were the scarce pool. With FP8, halves, so a slot costs as much as 3,144 cached tokens instead of 1,572, and there are tokens to spare. With 512 slots, the token pool shrinks to 2.48 M, still room for 74 agents, and up to 102 requests can run. At 64 agents the hit rate went from 60% to 91%, and the median wait from 19 s to 0.38 s. That is the first configuration in this post where 64 agents fit.

They fit, but they do not yet pass. The p90 wait at 64 is 3.4 s, and each user gets 15 tokens/s: R2 and R3 still fail.

Command: a smaller cache, a bigger state pool, and Q1 
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B \
  --context-length 131072 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --enable-metrics \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --max-mamba-cache-size 512      # or nvfp4; bf16 is the default

Q1 needs the model’s probabilities at every position of a continuation. SGLang returns them for prompt tokens too, from logprob_start_len on:

import requests
URL = "http://localhost:30000"

def tail_topk(context, continuation, k=20):
    requests.post(URL + "/generate", json={"input_ids": context, "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 1}})  # cache P
    r = requests.post(URL + "/generate", json={
        "input_ids": context + continuation, "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 1},
        "return_logprob": True, "logprob_start_len": len(context) - 1, "top_logprobs_num": k}).json()
    return r["meta_info"]["input_top_logprobs"]   # one top-k list per continuation position

Run it against each server, then compare the lists position by position.

Where this leaves me

Fewer bits buy what the napkin says they buy, and on Qwen3.5 they are close to free: FP8 passes R4, retrieval does not move, and with the state pool resized, 64 agents fit on one GPU. On Qwen3-8B the same trick doubles the agents and fails R4, because every rounding error in a key lands in attention’s exponent.

What none of it fixes is speed. Every running agent still reads its whole context on every step, and at 64 agents that is the bottleneck.

Chapter 6: Reading less

At 64 agents on Qwen3.5, each user gets 15 tokens/s. Chapter 0’s decode formula says why:

Every step reads all the weights once, plus every running agent’s whole cache. At = 64 agents of = 69K tokens, in FP8, that is 94 GB per step, or 65 ms at the bandwidth Chapter 0 measured: at most 15 tokens/s per user, exactly what the run got. R3 wants 30. There are two ways to change the formula. Read fewer of the tokens per step, or get more than one token out of each step.

Dropping tokens

The direct way to read less is to keep less. Token eviction throws away the cached tokens it guesses will not matter again, permanently. Two well-known guesses:

  • StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2024) keeps the first few tokens and a recent window. The first few matter because attention has to put its weight somewhere, and models learn to park spare weight on the first tokens (they are called attention sinks).
  • SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) keeps the recent window plus the older tokens that window attended to most. With the attention token pays to token , each old token is scored by , and the top ones stay.

An agent’s cache has to be compressed before its next turn exists, so I ran SnapKV without knowing the question: it scores the tokens by the attention of the context’s own last 32 tokens. SGLang does not evict tokens from inside a sequence, so this ran offline in PyTorch on Qwen3-8B, with 32K-token windows of code and the same KL as Chapter 5.

Nothing here passes R4 (3.6e-03). SnapKV at half the cache moves the model 2.4 times as far as allowed, about what FP8 did for the same 2× saving, and it gets much worse below half. StreamingLLM ignores what is in the context and is worse at every budget. Agent contexts do not have a recent part that matters and an old part that does not: the file read twenty turns ago is still the file being edited.

Reading only what matters

Eviction makes its guess once and lives with it. Sparse attention keeps the whole cache in memory and, at each step, reads only the parts that step needs. That saves no memory. It attacks the reads, which are what R3 is short of.

The bet is that attention is concentrated. If the blocks a step reads capture most of its attention weight, the output barely changes, because the output is a weighted average of values and the skipped ones had little weight. Write for the share of attention the best blocks capture:

How far could that go, in the best case? I measured it with an oracle. At each of 32 decode steps over a 32K-token context, I computed the real attention, picked the 64-token blocks that got the most of it in each layer, and reran the step with attention restricted to those blocks.

Put next to eviction, on the share of the cache each one uses:

Reading 12.5% of the context, the right 4,096 tokens, captures 93% of the attention and moves the model by 1.9e-03, inside R4. That is about the change FP8 made to Qwen3.5, for an eighth of the cache reads. Using an eighth is far better than keeping half, because the right eighth is different at every step, and eviction has to pick one set for all of them.

But it is an oracle. It needs the full attention to know which blocks to read, and the full attention is the read it is trying to avoid. Real sparse-attention methods guess the blocks from a cheap summary of each one, and they will miss some of that mass. SGLang 0.5.23 has nothing like it for these two models, so on this stack the saving stays on paper.

More tokens per read

The other way is to make each step produce more than one token. Qwen3.5 ships with a small extra head trained to guess the next few tokens (multi-token prediction). In speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), that head drafts tokens, and one step of the big model checks all of them at once: it computes what it would have written at each of the positions and keeps the drafts up to the first one it disagrees with. When most drafts are accepted, one read of the weights and the cache yields several tokens. With tokens kept per step,

and the step costs about the same as a normal one, as long as checking tokens instead of one does not run out of compute.

These are real code prompts, so the acceptance is honest: with 4 draft tokens, 4.2 are kept per step. With one request at a time, that is 2.5× the speed.

At 16 and 32 requests the gain is gone, and the napkin says why. Each request here is a 16K-token prompt with a 256-token reply. At 32 at a time, the server finished 1.0 requests per second, and prefilling their prompts alone needs 68% of the GPU’s compute. The GPU is busy with prefill, which speculation does not speed up, and the decode steps squeezed in between are long because they share the GPU with it. Checking 5 tokens instead of 1 then costs compute the GPU does not have.

Speculation also takes memory: the draft head and its own cache shrank the token pool from 1.64 M to 0.99 M. For many agents on one GPU, it is the wrong trade. For a few agents that need to be fast, it is the best one in this post.

A related worry was the hybrid’s fixed cost. Every Qwen3.5 request reads and writes its DeltaNet state, , every step, whatever the context length. At short contexts that could have made it slower than Qwen3-8B. It does not, measurably:

The same run also timed 8K and 32K contexts, but two of those points disagree with Chapter 0’s measurements of the same thing, so I left them out until I know why.

Command: speculative decoding with Qwen3.5’s own draft head 
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B \
  --context-length 131072 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --enable-metrics \
  --speculative-algorithm NEXTN --speculative-draft-model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B \
  --speculative-num-steps 4 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 5

The response’s meta_info reports spec_accept_length, the tokens kept per step. The server also caps running requests at 48 when speculation is on, and says so in its log.

Where a Qwen3.5 fork can start

Chapter 0 left a warning: a DeltaNet state is a blend of everything before it, so Qwen3.5 can only resume from a point where a snapshot was saved. Chapter 3’s forks all branched at the end of a turn, where one always is. A sub-agent can also branch from the middle of one, for example right after the planner wrote its plan but before the tool output that followed. I built a 4-turn parent with 4,096-token turns and forked it at positions on and off turn boundaries.

Qwen3-8B reuses the parent’s cache up to the exact token. Qwen3.5 reuses it only up to the last turn boundary, whatever snapshot interval I set: --mamba-track-interval of 64, 256 and 1024 tokens all gave the same row. The warning came true. SGLang saved a state at the end of each request, not every 64 tokens, and a fork inside the first turn reuses nothing at all.

Where this leaves me

The reads are the problem now, and on this stack they stay the problem. Dropping tokens fails R4 at any budget worth having. Reading only the right tokens would work, but only an oracle knows which they are, and SGLang does not offer the approximation for these models. Speculation helps a single agent by 2.5× and many agents not at all.

That leaves one direction from Chapter 2 untried: putting the caches that do not fit somewhere bigger than GPU memory.

Chapter 7: Bigger than GPU memory

Chapter 0 measured two places bigger than GPU memory (Table 10): this machine’s 176 GB of CPU memory, behind a 57 GB/s link, and a disk at 1.7 GB/s. Chapter 3 showed what needs them: the caches of parked agents, which the GPU pool keeps evicting. SGLang can put both behind the pool as tiers (--enable-hierarchical-cache). A cache evicted from the GPU is kept in CPU memory, and when its agent comes back, it is copied back instead of recomputed.

Whether that pays is a race between a copy and a rebuild. For an agent returning with private tokens:

For one synthetic agent’s 33K private tokens on Qwen3-8B, the copy moves 4.9 GB:

CPU memory wins by a mile. The disk is roughly a wash with recomputing.

CPU memory

--hicache-ratio sets the CPU pool’s size as a multiple of the GPU pool’s. I ran Chapter 2’s synthetic sweep with ratios 1 and 2 on both models, out to 96 agents.

Ratio 1 does almost nothing for Qwen3-8B, and that is by design. By default SGLang copies every page to the CPU pool as soon as it is computed (write-through), so the CPU pool holds a copy of the GPU pool before it holds anything else. With a GPU pool and ratio , what the two tiers hold between them is

At ratio 1, that is just : the copy is all it holds. At ratio 2 there is a second pool’s worth of room, and the hit rate holds at 91% out to 32 agents, where without it the cliff was at 16.

The hits did not bring the wait down, though: 42 s at 32 agents. That is Chapter 3’s lesson from the other side. CPU memory can keep a parked agent’s cache. But a running request still needs its whole context in GPU memory, and Qwen3-8B’s GPU pool runs about 13 synthetic agents at a time. Past that they queue, cache or no cache. The CPU tier turns their rebuild into a copy. It does not give them a seat.

Qwen3.5 has the bigger GPU pool, so it gets the seats. With ratio 2 it keeps a 94% hit rate and a 0.6 s median wait at 64 agents, in BF16 with the old 256 state slots. At 96 it queues again: 51 running at most, Chapter 5’s limit. Ratio 1 already helped at 48 agents on Qwen3.5, which the write-through copy does not explain. I have not looked into why.

When to copy

If write-through spends the CPU pool on copies, the policy should matter. --hicache-write-policy has three settings. Write-through copies every page. Write-through-selective copies only pages that have been hit a few times. Write-back copies a page only when the GPU evicts it, so the CPU pool holds nothing the GPU still has:

Same point, 48 agents on Qwen3-8B, ratio 2:

Write-back turns the same CPU memory into half again as much unique capacity, and the hit rate goes from 70% to 90%. Selective is the worst of the three. My reading is that an agent’s cache is used by one agent a few times, so “hit often” rarely singles one out, and most of them never reach the CPU pool at all. The wait improved too, 196 s to 150 s, but it is still minutes, for the reason above: 48 agents is far past what Qwen3-8B can run at once.

For agents, the default is the wrong choice. Write-through’s advantage is that a page already has its copy when the GPU evicts it, so eviction never waits on the link.

The disk

Below CPU memory, SGLang’s file backend writes pages to disk and prefetches them back when a request matches them. --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy decides whether a request waits for the whole prefetch (wait_complete), takes what has arrived (best_effort), or waits up to a timeout. I ran 48 and 96 agents on Qwen3-8B with a CPU pool of ratio 1 and the disk behind it.

The disk changed nothing, which is what Figure 26 said: a page from disk costs about what recomputing it does, and these agents are queued for seats anyway.

One caveat on this run. SGLang ignores its own flags for where the file backend writes, and takes the directory only from the environment variable SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR. Without it, pages go to /tmp/hicache, which here grew to 415 GB, and my harness emptied a different directory between policies. So the second and third policies started with the first one’s pages on disk. That can only have helped them, and they still gained nothing.

Command: CPU and disk tiers 
export SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR=/data/hicache   # otherwise /tmp/hicache, with no size limit
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --json-model-override-args '{"rope_scaling":{"rope_type":"yarn","factor":4.0,"original_max_position_embeddings":32768},"max_position_embeddings":131072}' \
  --context-length 131072 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --enable-metrics \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 2 --hicache-write-policy write_back \
  --hicache-storage-backend file --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete   # the disk tier; drop for CPU only

The response’s meta_info.cached_tokens_details splits each hit into device, host and storage tokens.

item.title: Does RL in autoregressive decoding move the benchmark needle in diffusion decoding?
item.description:
First things first, this new model by NVIDIA, Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-3B, blew my mind. It can generate text in two ways: one token at a time, like a regular language model (autoregressive, or AR mode), and several tokens at once (diffusion mode). Both modes use the same model weights.

The speed is what excites me. But I haven’t come across a post-training recipe for diffusion transformers that feels mainstream yet. How do I take one of these fast models and make it better at a task?

We already have recipes for post-training autoregressive models. What if I post-train this model in AR mode, then switch it back to diffusion? Does any of that improvement carry over?

If it does, that would be insanely valuable: I could use a familiar training setup to improve the model, then use its faster diffusion mode to generate answers. That could be extremely useful in production applications, where I want a model that’s good at the task and responds quickly. Of course, sharing weights doesn’t guarantee that the gains transfer.

Experiment design

For this run, I use reinforcement learning (RL) to train only the AR mode. I save checkpoints along the way and try each one in both modes. Step 0 is the original model, before any training.

I wanted problems with room to improve and answers I could check automatically.

The tech report reports 87.9% on GSM8K in AR mode and 88.4% in diffusion mode for the 3B instruct model. There’s less room to improve there, so I kept GSM8K as a check and looked for harder problems to train on.

For MATH, I tried 300 problems each from Levels 3, 4 and 5 of the test set in AR mode:

MATH level AR accuracy
Level 3 84.3%
Level 4 75.7%
Level 5 59.3%

Level 5 it is. Diffusion mode on the same 300 problems got 56.3% using NVIDIA’s HF implementation. Those probe scores helped me pick the task; the larger checkpoint sweep below uses SGLang for diffusion.

Here’s the training and eval setup:

Part of the experiment Setup
Model Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-3B
Training AR-only RL on MATH train Levels 4 and 5: 3,994 problems
Testing on MATH 500 MATH Level-5 problems from the test split
Checking GSM8K 200 GSM8K test questions, outside the training dataset
Checkpoints evaluated Original model, then steps 25, 50, 75, 100, 125 and 150

I didn’t train on GSM8K. I keep those questions around to check whether training on MATH also changes how the model handles another set of problems, especially whether it makes those answers worse.

Each checkpoint gets the same test questions, with greedy decoding and one answer per question. I count how many answers are right. For MATH, math-verify parses the prediction and checks it against the gold solution. For GSM8K, I check the last number in the last <answer> tag, falling back to the last number in the output if the tag is missing.

The instructions go in a single user message; I don’t add a custom system prompt. For MATH, I use the same prompt during training and evaluation in both modes:

{problem}

Think step by step, then put the final answer in \boxed{}.

For the GSM8K check:

{question}

Think step by step, then give the final number inside <answer> </answer> tags.

Both use the model’s chat template with enable_thinking=False.

I shuffle the MATH test questions with seed 1234 before selecting them; GSM8K keeps its original test order. The pinned revisions are 0530c786 for MATH, 740312ad for GSM8K and 0d51902d for the model. AR runs through vLLM, diffusion through SGLang. Each mode keeps the same engine and settings across checkpoints.

Training setup

Before getting to GRPO, it helps to unpack how this model can do both jobs. In the paper, NVIDIA trains a shared transformer with two objectives: predict the next token from the tokens before it, and recover missing tokens inside a block. The same weights learn both.

The attention mask controls which tokens can see each other:

  • AR mode: causal attention limits each position to itself and earlier positions; the model predicts the next token from that prefix. Generation proceeds left to right.
  • Diffusion mode: positions inside the current block can attend to each other and the completed prefix. The model fills masked positions over several passes, committing confident predictions. Blocks still finish in order; the whole answer isn’t generated at once. I use 32-token blocks here.

The paper calls this a tri-mode model because it also supports self-speculation: diffusion drafts tokens and AR verifies them. This experiment uses the two modes separately.

For the 3B checkpoint, the implementation wraps a Ministral3 transformer and an output layer that turns its hidden states into scores over the vocabulary. That transformer is stored under encoder, and the output layer under diffusion_head. Both are used by the AR path too, despite those names.

Now the practical problem: I’m using TRL’s GRPO trainer with vLLM to generate the training answers. I need those tools to load the checkpoint as a causal language model. NVIDIA ships a custom model class with its own AR and diffusion generation methods, so I can’t just point my usual training setup at it and assume it’ll work.

But I only need the AR path for training. Since that path uses the Ministral3 backbone, I can save the weights in the layout expected by Ministral3ForCausalLM, which my training stack can load.

What the conversion changes

The conversion renames the weight keys and writes a matching Ministral3 model config:

NVIDIA checkpoint AR checkpoint used by the trainer
encoder.* model.*
diffusion_head.* lm_head.*

The weight values and tokenizer stay the same. This export gives the trainer the AR view of the model; it doesn’t provide diffusion generation. To evaluate a trained checkpoint in diffusion mode, I reverse the names and load the updated weights with NVIDIA’s original config and model code.

Before training, I checked the original AR path against the converted model on the same prompt. The largest logit difference was 0.0, and greedy decoding produced the same tokens. That check gave me confidence to use the converted checkpoint for the run. GRPO then updates those shared weights through AR answers; afterward, I load them back into the original model to see what happened to diffusion.

The RL itself is plain GRPO in TRL, with vLLM generating the rollouts:

  • 64 problems per step, 8 answers each, so 512 rollouts per step
  • learning rate 1e-6, no KL penalty, temperature 1.0, up to 2,048 tokens per answer
  • reward is 1 for a correct answer, 0 otherwise
  • a checkpoint every 25 steps
VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 uv run accelerate launch --config_file configs/fsdp8.yaml -m dar.train_grpo \
  --task math --run-name math-ar-grpo \
  --hypothesis "RL in AR mode also raises diffusion-mode accuracy on the same task" --vllm-mem 0.4

The training run

Training took about 34 seconds per step. I planned 200 steps, but the trainer’s own check (AR mode, 128 test problems, one sampled answer each) went flat around step 100, so I stopped it after 164 logged training steps. The last checkpoint is step 150.

The reward goes from about 0.62 over the first 10 steps to about 0.74 after step 100. The answers also get a lot longer, from about 735 tokens to about 1,100. By steps 51 to 100, about 21% of the rollouts were hitting the 2,048-token limit.

Results

And… it moves. Diffusion goes from 51.8% to between 55.2% and 59.0%, depending on the checkpoint. AR goes from 59.2% to between 63.0% and 66.8%.

Across the six checkpoints, AR gains 5.6 points on average and diffusion gains 5.3. Almost the same gain, even though diffusion never saw a masked block during training.

I also checked which of the 500 problems each checkpoint fixed or broke compared with step 0, using a McNemar test. For diffusion, the change from step 0 is significant at p < 0.05 at steps 25, 75, 125 and 150 (p = 0.007, 0.014, 0.002, 0.031). At steps 50 and 100 it isn’t (p = 0.09 and 0.16). AR is significant at every checkpoint except step 75 (p = 0.08). Those are unadjusted p-values across six checkpoint comparisons per mode. These checkpoints share a training run and test questions, so they aren’t independent experiments.

The gap doesn’t close, though. Diffusion is 7.4 points behind AR at step 0 and 8.0 behind at step 150.

GSM8K

On GSM8K, AR goes from 87.5% to between 88.0% and 91.5%, and diffusion from 86.5% to between 87.0% and 89.5%. None of the changes from step 0 is statistically significant. I don’t see a clear regression here, but 200 questions can’t rule out smaller changes or tell me what happens on other tasks.

Running out of tokens

The longer answers run into the token limit at eval time too.

At step 0, 26 AR answers and 22 diffusion answers ran out of room. From step 50 on it’s between 93 and 138 in each mode, so a fifth to a quarter of all answers get cut off before they reach a \boxed{}. I looked at the cut-off diffusion answers from step 75, and they aren’t loops, they’re just long, careful markdown solutions that run out of tokens.

RL is partly fighting its own length here: TRL drops truncated completions from the loss.

I also caught a mismatch while writing this: the AR eval in vLLM had a 2,048-token context, so the answer budget was 2,048 minus the prompt (45 to 1,087 tokens). Diffusion got 2,048 new tokens. Longer answers after training mean that mismatch can affect the measured gains too. I’ve fixed the budget setup for the next run.

I’d like to try this with a bigger answer budget and more seeds. This was one run of one 3B model, and I used the test split to pick a difficulty level and monitor training. Next time, those decisions need a separate set.

Eval settings

For the first diffusion numbers I used NVIDIA’s HF generate() with block size 32 and confidence threshold 0.9, which is what the model card shows. It works, but it decodes one problem at a time. On 300 Level-5 problems it ran at about 77 tokens/s per GPU. At that rate, evaluating 7 checkpoints × 700 problems would take too long.

At the time of this run, the vLLM diffusion path I looked at supported DiffusionGemma, and each model brought its own sampler, so using this model there would have needed a port. NVIDIA’s own serving code is an SGLang PR, sgl-project/sglang#25803, which adds this model with FastDiffuser (plain diffusion mode) plus CUDA graphs and batching. I built that branch in its own environment, since it wants torch 2.11, with the same settings as the HF run: 32-token blocks, threshold 0.9, a causal pass to seed each block.

Getting it to start on this box took three fixes, all on the environment side. There’s no CUDA toolkit on the node, so I pointed CUDA_HOME at the one that ships in the venv. FlashInfer tried to compile its kernels and failed, so I installed its prebuilt kernels the same way the PR’s Dockerfile does. And pip had pulled a CUDA 13.4 compiler next to a 13.0 runtime, so I pinned the compiler packages back to 13.0.

After that: about 1,340 tokens/s per GPU. 300 problems in 97 seconds.

But the accuracy didn’t match. On the same 300 problems SGLang got 52.3%, HF got 56.3%. Only 27 of the 300 answers were word for word the same, and the rest split after about 400 characters (the median), which is consistent with greedy decoding diverging after small numerical differences between engines. I did not isolate the cause. On the problems where they disagree, HF alone was right on 32 and SGLang alone on 20. That’s a McNemar p of about 0.10, so the gap could be noise, but I can’t call it zero either. So the rule from here on: every checkpoint goes through SGLang, and I only compare SGLang numbers with SGLang numbers.

Data behind the charts

The CSVs used in the charts are here: checkpoint evaluations, training metrics, trainer evaluations, and task and engine probes. The paired-test p-values are recorded in the checkpoint export; the per-problem outputs are not included here.

item.title: Worklog: Post training Qwen2.5 for math reasoning
item.description:
It’s been a while since I wanted to write a worklog like this, where I walk through the actual process of training models for xyz task. So in this blog, we are gonna train a model for high school maths. And we picked Qwen2.5-0.5B as our candidate model, deliberately for two reasons: 1. It’s pretty small, smallest in category of LLMs. 2. It was never trained to reason.

So throughout this worklog, we train this smol model to reason, and solve maths problems.

And one more thing, it is not gonna be another tutorial where I just give you bunch of lines of code to train a model, and expect model to be magically SoTA, because in reality it doesn’t work like that, haha. So, in case if you are new to RL, you will get a taste of how does training this models look like.

This worklog uses code from this huggingface tutorial, except system prompt is little different.

Alright, let’s formalize the problem. Let’s say for a question: Tobias is buying a new pair of shoes that costs $95. He has been saving up his money each month for the past three months. He gets a $5 allowance a month. He also mows lawns and shovels driveways. He charges $15 to mow a lawn and $7 to shovel. After buying the shoes, he has $15 in change. If he mows 4 lawns, how many driveways did he shovel?

I want my model to respond like this:

<start_working_out>
He saved up $110 total because 95 + 15 = <<95+15=110>>110
He saved $15 from his allowance because 3 x 5 = <<3*5=15>>15
He earned $60 mowing lawns because 4 x 15 = <<4*15=60>>60
He earned $35 shoveling driveways because 110 - 60 - 15 = <<110-60-15=35>>35
He shoveled 5 driveways because 35 / 7 = <<35/7=5>>5
<end_working_out>
<SOLUTION>5</SOLUTION>

Baselines first

Before training anything, I wanted to know where the model starts. So I wrote the system prompt that every run in this worklog uses:

You are a mathematical reasoning assistant.
When given a math problem:
1. Show the calculations and step by step solution between <start_working_out> and <end_working_out>
2. Give the final answer between <SOLUTION> and </SOLUTION>

Do not use \boxed{}. Do not write anything after </SOLUTION>.

Example:
<start_working_out>
Shelf one has 35 books and shelf two has 18.
35 + 18 = 53
<end_working_out>
<SOLUTION>53</SOLUTION>

The worked example and the “no \boxed{}” line are there for a reason. My first version of this prompt had neither, and when I tried it on a Qwen3 model, it got 80% of the math right but wrapped 97% of its answers in \boxed{} instead of the tags. A strict parser scored it 4%. One example fixed that.

Then I ran Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on the full GSM8K test set (1,319 questions) with greedy decoding, and my benchmark script printed this:

accuracy (mean@1): 0.0000   (strict: script's answer format)
accuracy lenient:  0.3776   (any \boxed / #### / last number)

Zero. For a second I thought the model couldn’t follow the format at all. It turned out my benchmark script’s “strict” check was looking for a #### <number> line (from an older prompt), not the <SOLUTION> tags. So I re-scored the same 1,319 answers with the checks I was actually going to train with:

Checks Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct
right number anywhere in the answer 37.7%
right number inside <SOLUTION> 17.5%
exact tag format 27.3%
right answer and exact format 11.5%

I also benchmarked Qwen3-0.6B on the test set before training. It scored 36%.

So the model can do the math on more than a third of the problems, but less than half of those right answers land where a parser can find them. Less than half of its answers (43%) even had a <SOLUTION> block. That gap between “can do the math” and “writes it down the way I asked” kept coming back through this whole worklog.

Getting the first run to train at all

The cookbook is written for a single consumer GPU, so it loads the model in 4-bit and lets device_map="auto" place it. My very first run crashed before step 1:

torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 49.99 GiB.

50 GB, for a 0.5B model. It turns out the loss computes fp32 scores over Qwen’s whole 152k-token vocabulary, for every token of every completion. With completions allowed up to 2,048 tokens and 8 of them per GPU, that one tensor is huge. GSM8K answers are about 200 tokens long, so I cut the limit to 512.

I also dropped 4-bit (at 0.5B parameters I had enough memory without it) and device_map="auto", which fights accelerate when you want one copy of the model per GPU. The final setup: vLLM on GPU 0 generating the rollouts, the remaining GPUs training, LoRA on the cookbook’s q_proj and v_proj, and the cookbook’s learning rate (5e-6) and gradient clipping (0.1). I kept TRL’s default loss_type="dapo" for the GRPO runs.

Naive rewards: correctness and format

My first real run, jr8dtkxv, used the two most obvious rewards:

  1. correctness: 1 if the number inside <SOLUTION> matches the answer, else 0.
  2. format: 1 if the whole completion has the exact tag structure, else 0.

Writing even these two, I shipped two bugs on the first try. The reference answers in GSM8K end with #### 72, but I was parsing them with the same function that looks for <SOLUTION>, so every reference answer came out as None. And TRL wants one reward per completion, but my function returned a single number for the whole batch. Fun.

With those fixed, I trained on the full training set (7,473 questions), 8 samples per question, for 300 steps. And… nothing.

Correctness started at 8.1% and ended at 7.6%. On the test set it sat at 6.8%. (Test numbers during training are sampled at temperature 1.0, so they come in lower than the greedy 17.5% from the baseline.) Format hovered around 20%.

So I opened the rollout table in W&B, the one TRL fills with every prompt, completion and reward. 91% of the rollouts were wrong, and 76% of the wrong ones had no <SOLUTION> block at all. A lot of them looked like this one:

Q: Pat’s Pool Supply has three times as many swimming pools as Pat’s Ark & Athletic Wear store. If Pat’s Ark & Athletic Wear store has 200 pools, how many pools do they have in total?

<start_working_out>
Let's break this down step by step:
...
3. So, Pat's Pool Supply has 3 * 200 = 600 swimming pools.
4. Now, we add the number of pools both stores have: 200 + 600 = 800 pools.

That means they have 800 pools altogether.

The answer is 800. The model got it right, then never closed the working-out block and never wrote <SOLUTION>, so it scored zero.

The same table showed a second problem. GRPO learns by comparing the samples within a group, so a question where all 8 samples score the same gives it nothing to learn from. 57.5% of the groups were 0/8, and exactly one group out of 2,114 was 8/8.

GRPO doesn’t update toward an answer just because it got a reward. It compares each answer’s reward with the other seven, using an advantage like this in the original GRPO formulation:

Here, is one answer’s reward; and are the mean and standard deviation across the eight answers. For the correctness reward, a 0/8 group has eight zeros, so every reward equals the mean. An 8/8 group has eight ones, and again every reward equals the mean. Either way, every advantage is zero. The update is multiplied by that advantage, so correctness gives the model no direction: it can’t tell which answer to make more likely. The same thing happens any time all eight answers get the same total reward. I also had a format reward, though, so an all-wrong group could still give a signal if some answers followed the format and others didn’t.

Filtering the 0/8 and 8/8 questions

If most questions teach nothing, why train on them? I wrote a script that downloads a run’s rollout tables from W&B, groups them per question, and drops the questions that came out 0/8 or 8/8. jr8dtkxv had seen 2,100 questions: 1,206 were all-wrong and 1 all-right, so 1,207 went out. I also cut the group size from 8 to 4, to cover more questions per step, and launched dszbz193.

Flat again. Correctness went from 10.9% to 10.8%, test correctness stayed at 7%. This time I looked at the optimizer instead of the rewards:

Three things were stacked against me, all straight from the cookbook’s single-GPU defaults:

  • Learning rate 5e-6. That’s a full fine-tuning learning rate. LoRA usually needs about 10× more.
  • Gradient clipping at 0.1. The gradient norm averaged 0.13, so 79% of the steps were clipped.
  • LoRA only on q_proj and v_proj. Very few trainable weights.

I went to 3e-5, clipping at 1.0, and LoRA on every linear layer. I also set lora_dropout to 0, after the terminal showed an importance-sampling ratio of 0.16 during a test run. More on that ratio later, because it turned out to be the biggest problem in this whole worklog.

Presampling: pass@k before training

Filtering from a run’s logs had a hole: it only knew about the questions that run happened to sample, 2,100 of 7,473. So instead of mining old rollouts, I wrote presampling script. Before training even starts, it generates samples for every training question (with vLLM, about a minute), scores them, and drops the ones with no learnable signal. The point of RL is to amplify the signal the model already has, and a question it always gets right, or never gets right, has none.

For this first presample I used 4 samples per question, and it gave me a scare: 5,330 of the 7,473 questions came out 0/4. But I had seen this movie already. Most “wrong” answers were format failures, not math failures. So I also scored them leniently, counting the answer if the right number was the last number anywhere in the text. 45% of the “0/4” questions turned out to be right math in the wrong place. With lenient scoring, 2,950 questions were 0/4 and 426 were 4/4, which left 4,097 to train on.

The model was struggling with both format and correctness, and the two all-or-nothing rewards gave it no credit for being close on either. So for this run I added three rewards:

  • tag_check (weight 1.0): 0.125 for each of the four tags that appears exactly once, max 0.5. Partial credit for getting the format partly right. A tag repeated twice earns nothing, so it can’t be farmed.
  • lenient_correctness_check (weight 0.5): right number anywhere. Right math in the wrong place should beat wrong math.
  • exact_check (weight 2.0): right answer and exact format. The thing I actually want gets the biggest reward.

That was iql9rc9t.

The total reward went up (0.75 to 0.90), but mostly from the partial rewards. Format went from 22% to 30%, correctness on training batches from 11.8% to 14.4%. On the test set: 6.1% to 6.9% exact. Something was moving, but barely.

One panel did change completely: the share of groups with no learning signal dropped from about 35% to 1%. Almost every group now had samples with different scores. So the model had plenty of signal, and it still wasn’t learning much from it.

More partial rewards

Looking at the rollouts again, two kinds of failure were left.

First, on hard questions the model got the final answer wrong but was sometimes halfway there, and nothing gave it credit for that. GSM8K’s reference solutions mark every calculation, like <<48/2=24>>. So step_check takes those intermediate results (skipping the final answer and anything already in the question) and gives credit for the fraction that show up in the reasoning. If a completion contains way more numbers than a real solution would, the credit shrinks, so dumping numbers doesn’t pay. Before using it I checked it on saved rollouts: in 56% of groups every sample had the same correctness, and step_check still gave different scores within 85% of those.

Second, the <SOLUTION> tag sometimes held things like $10 + $2. instead of a number, which breaks the parser even when the math is right. So solution_number_check gives a small reward when the tag holds just a number.

That made the full set, max 5.25:

Reward Gives 1 when Weight Why I added it
exact_check right answer and exact format 2.0 the actual target
correctness_check right number inside <SOLUTION> 1.0 the original signal
lenient_correctness_check right number anywhere 0.5 credit the math even when the format fails
format_check exact tag structure 0.5 the original format signal
tag_check 0.125 per tag present exactly once (max 0.5) 1.0 credit a partly right format
step_check fraction of the reference’s intermediate results reached 0.5 credit being halfway there
solution_number_check <SOLUTION> holds just a number 0.25 keep the answer parseable

I also redid the presample with 8 samples per question, to match the group size in training: 2,009 questions were 0/8 and 84 were 8/8, leaving 5,380.

The first launch crashed on step 1, with step_check complaining it never got its steps column. The datasets library had cached my preprocessed dataset from before I added that column. It recognizes a function it has seen by its name, not its code, so my edit never took effect. One load_from_cache_file=False later, it trained: cr6hatom.

Reward 1.18 to 1.25. Test exact accuracy 5.6% to 6.3% over 444 steps. Seven rewards, every group with a learning signal, and the model had barely moved.

Same recipe, Qwen3-0.6B

At this point I had two suspects: my rewards, or the model. So at the same time, I kicked off the exact same setup with Qwen3-0.6B (thinking mode off): same prompt, same seven rewards, same hyperparameters, its own 8-sample presample (1,336 questions 0/8, 912 8/8, 5,225 left). That’s 9ue7k08w. Qwen3 had scored 36% on the test set before training, so I had a baseline for this comparison too.

And it just… worked. Reward climbed from 3.47 to 4.45 out of 5.25. Exact accuracy on training batches went from 55% to 82%, format from 86% to 98%. On the test set, exact accuracy was 64.8% at step 100 and 67.2% at step 200. The share of groups with no signal climbed from 7% to 36%, the good kind of rising: the model was starting to get whole groups right.

So the rewards were fine. Now I wanted the same thing from Qwen2.5.

SFT warm-up

Qwen2.5 was clearly struggling with the format, the RL reward was flat, and piling on small partial rewards hadn’t fixed it. So before RL, I decided to just show it the format with supervised fine-tuning.

For data, I used the 2,093 questions the presample had eliminated (2,009 always wrong, 84 always right). RL wasn’t using them anyway, and this way the SFT data can’t contaminate the RL data. I rewrote their GSM8K reference solutions into my tag format and checked that all 7,473 rewritten solutions score 1.0 on my format and correctness rewards, so the model learns exactly what RL would reward.

The first SFT run looked healthy for 30 steps, then the gradient norm turned into NaN, the loss dropped to exactly 0, and it quietly saved a model whose every single weight was NaN:

My first guess was precision, so I kept fp32 master weights and added a guard that stops the run on the first NaN. It stopped at step 30 again, same step. That was the hint: the data order is seeded, so step 30 always gets the same batch. Each of the 2,093 examples was fine on its own. But replaying TRL’s batching on one GPU, batch 232 gave a finite loss and NaN gradients, and only through PyTorch’s SDPA attention kernel in bf16. The same batch with SDPA in fp32, or with eager attention, was fine. I switched to eager attention and SFT went through cleanly (rylnmvbk).

After SFT, the model is a different model, so I presampled again with the same scoring as before: 1,705 questions 0/8 and 274 8/8. I dropped those, plus the 2,093 SFT questions, leaving 4,380 for RL. Then 6hqxh39p:

Immediate jump. The reward started at 3.0 instead of 1.2, and format was basically solved: 99% on training batches, 99.3% on the test set. Completions got shorter too, about 105 tokens instead of 180. Correctness, though, only moved a little: 42% to 48% on training batches, and 22.8% exact on the test set. Up from 6%, but RL on top was flat again.

OPD warm-up

SFT was one warm-up. For a separate experiment, I wanted to try something that could teach the reasoning too, so I used on-policy distillation (OPD) instead. The student writes its own answers, a bigger teacher scores every token of them, and the student learns to move toward the teacher’s choices, token by token.

OPD and SFT give dense feedback on every token, where RL gives one number per answer.

The teacher was Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. With my prompt it gets 91.7% of the training questions right and 77% in exact format, so it pulls the student toward exactly what my rewards want. (One snag: its vocabulary has 152,064 rows and the student’s 151,936, and TRL refuses to distill across different sizes. Both use the same tokenizer with 151,665 real tokens, so the extra rows are unused padding. Trimming them left the teacher’s probabilities unchanged.)

Same 2,093 questions as the SFT, 3fjg9zef:

The presample after OPD looked very different: only 861 questions 0/8, and 1,497 already 8/8. After dropping those and the OPD questions, 3,763 were left for RL. c0uc1sfx:

More gains: exact accuracy on training batches around 57–59%, and 40.8% on the test set, almost double the SFT warm-up. But look at the test accuracy across the whole run: 40.8%, 40.4%, 40.3%, 40.8%, 40.0%, 40.5%, 40.9%, 41.1%. Eight hundred steps of RL, and nothing.

And this is where I finally noticed the panel I had been ignoring since the very first run: the importance-sampling ratio.

The importance-sampling ratio

In this setup there are two copies of the model. vLLM generates the rollouts, the trainer computes the gradients, and after every update the trainer pushes its new weights to vLLM. In theory both copies are the same model, so they should give every token the same probability. In practice their code is different (different kernels, different rounding), so TRL checks: for every sampled token, it compares vLLM’s probability with the trainer’s, and multiplies those ratios over the whole completion. With its default setting, sequence_mask, a completion whose ratio drifts too far from 1 is simply dropped from the loss.

The sequence ratio

Written out, it’s just the product of the token ratios:

sequence_mask uses that one ratio for the whole completion. If it falls outside the configured range, TRL drops the whole completion (docs). That’s why a small mismatch at each token can add up, especially on a long answer.

So this number decides how much of each batch the model actually learns from. The mean in the plot isn’t itself the fraction of completions kept: with sequence_mask, TRL makes that decision one completion at a time. But as the copies drift apart, longer answers have more chances for those token-level differences to compound and push the sequence ratio out of range.

Once I knew what to look for, it was everywhere:

It had been there since jr8dtkxv (0.92 falling to 0.36). Qwen3 started at 1.0 and never went below 0.6. Every Qwen2.5 run fell to somewhere between 0.3 and 0.55, most of them within the first 100 steps.

So why Qwen2.5 is worse at this and not Qwen3

The first thing I checked: is Qwen2.5 just more sensitive to bf16 rounding? No. 

The base model’s bf16 and fp32 versions differ by 0.043 nats per token, and Qwen3’s by 0.039. Basically the same.

The difference was in which tokens they sample. Rounding noise is tiny on tokens the model is sure about and much bigger on unlikely ones, because a small error in a small probability is a big error in its logarithm space. I measured it on 24 real vLLM-sampled completions per model:

Probability of the sampled token Noise per token Share of tokens, Qwen2.5 Share of tokens, Qwen3
above 0.9 (sure) ~0.001 57% 69%
0.5 – 0.9 ~0.015–0.019 20% 16%
0.1 – 0.5 ~0.04 14% 11%
below 0.1 (unlikely picks) ~0.05–0.06 9.5% 4.5%

Same noise curve for both models, but Qwen2.5 is less sure of itself on this task, so it picks about twice as many unlikely tokens. Its answers are also longer (210 tokens against 155 in this sample). Summed over a completion, the mismatch came out 2.88 for Qwen2.5 against 1.66 for Qwen3. Multiply that over a whole answer, and sequence_mask drops it.

Attempt 1: stop dropping whole answers

The obvious fix was TRL’s token_truncate mode: weight each token by its own ratio, capped at 3, instead of dropping entire completions. 6oyljev3:

For about 80 steps the ratio sat near 1, very stable, unlike any run before. But underneath, the mismatch was climbing the whole time (look at the log scale): from 0.02 nats per token at the start to 10 around step 100, and 4.8 by the end. Once it got that big, the ratio collapsed too. The gradient norm went from 0.2 to 1.4 and entropy collapsed from 0.28 to 0.09.

With sequence_mask, the samples where the two copies disagreed had been getting thrown away.

With token_truncate, the model kept training on them, and the two copies drifted further apart with every step. The rewards didn’t move either way.

Attempt 2: vLLM was running out of memory

The vLLM server’s log had lines like this every few syncs:

memory allocation failed with OOM on device 0 while trying to allocate 989855744 bytes

989,855,744 bytes is exactly Qwen2.5-0.5B in bf16. By default trl vllm-serve reserves 90% of the GPU for itself, and every weight sync tries to allocate a buffer the size of the whole model on top of that. The sync still returned 200 OK. So I gave vLLM 50% of the GPU instead and relaunched, 46in4jdn:

Same story: stable for about 100 steps, then the mismatch ran away to 4.9. The OOM was a problem, but it wasn’t the cause.

Attempt 3: fp32 everywhere

Then I started measuring precision directly, and found a few real problems:

  • The OPD checkpoint hates bf16. Converted to bf16, it drifts from its own fp32 version by 0.43 nats per token, against 0.047 for the base model. OPD trained it in fp32, but RL ran it in bf16, so RL started from a damaged version of it.
  • The weight sync rounds away most of the update. At every sync, TRL merges the LoRA update into the base weights and sends the result to vLLM in bf16. On my saved adapters, 49 - 62% of the weights didn’t change at all after the merge: the update was smaller than bf16’s resolution and rounded right back to the original value. The effect on probabilities was small though, about 0.013–0.018 nats per token.
  • Merging and unmerging in bf16 leaks. After 10 merge/unmerge round trips, the trainer’s own base weights had drifted by 2.5e-4 (relative). In fp32: 4e-9.

So I ran the whole thing in fp32, trainer and vLLM both, and went back to sequence_mask: i7yh9cby.

The start was much better, because the OPD model finally ran the way it was trained: 67% exact on training batches at step 0 instead of about 57%, and 47.9% exact on the test set, the best Qwen2.5 number in this worklog. The runaway was gone too.

But RL on top was still flat (47.9%, 48.4%, 48.6%), and the ratio still fell to about 0.42. So I looked at the first few steps, where the two copies should be identical:

At step 1 the mismatch was 0.00056, so vLLM and the trainer agreed almost perfectly. Then it grew by about 0.003 with every step: 0.006, 0.009, 0.012, 0.016… Qwen3 held flat over the same steps.

A mismatch that starts at zero and grows with every update means the two copies stop agreeing because of training. So I took the adapter checkpoints i7yh9cby had saved and tested every piece of the weight sync on its own, in fp32:

Test vLLM vs correct model (nats/token)
vLLM vs Hugging Face, same tokens, no training 0.0007 for Qwen2.5, 0.0008 for Qwen3
TRL-style padded batches, train mode, gradient checkpointing 0.0007
trainer’s unmerged LoRA vs merged weights 0.00000
one sync through vLLM’s weight loader (eager and compiled) 0.0008
three back-to-back syncs into a live trl vllm-serve 0.0008, no growth

Every piece checked out. So I tried the things only the live run has:

  • One GPU instead of seven (blyv9d73), in case the seven training processes were drifting apart. Still grew, the same way.
  • Less memory for vLLM. During that run vLLM swung between 44 and 70 GB on a 40 GB budget, and the OOM was back (545,259,520 bytes, exactly the embedding matrix in fp32). So I cut it to 25% (cpgrs28e). Still grew: 0.0006 to about 0.02 in 20 steps.

Taking vLLM out of the loop

Every piece of the sync checked out on its own, and the live loop still drifted. So the next morning I tried the simplest possible test: get rid of the second copy. TRL can also generate the rollouts with the training model itself, using plain Hugging Face generate. Slower, but there is only one copy of the policy, so nothing to sync, nothing to drift, and no importance-sampling correction at all. Same SFT checkpoint and same data as 6hqxh39p, temperature 1.0, fp32.

My first attempt, gv11dzpk, I killed after 23 steps. It looked the same as before, so I decided vLLM wasn’t the problem after all. That was a bad call. 23 steps at 16 questions a step is noise, and it hadn’t even reached its first test evaluation. So I ran it properly: gdi2sbor.

And there it was. For the first time in this whole worklog, RL itself was moving Qwen2.5. Exact accuracy on training batches climbed from 46% to 73%, and on the test set:

36.5% at step 100 and 42.2% at step 200, against a flat 22.8% → 22.5% with vLLM. Same checkpoint, same data, same rewards. The only difference was where the rollouts came from.

It wasn’t free, though. The first test evaluation took forever: 1,319 questions × 8 samples, generated 8 at a time, is about 165 generate calls per GPU. I raised the eval batch to 64 per GPU (same metric, about 21 calls) and turned on TF32 matmuls for fp32 runs without vLLM (no second copy to disagree with anymore).

So what’s wrong with my vLLM setup?

TRL’s vLLM server mode is used by a lot of people, so a drift this steady smelled like something in my setup. I went through TRL’s source: which model gets synced (the right one), when (before every generation, every step), with what names (the right ones), and with what sampling settings (top_k=0 and top_p=1, so no truncation bias). All fine.

Two things stood out, though. First, Qwen3’s mismatch had grown too, from 0.012 to 0.029 over its run. It just hid under bf16 noise early on. So it’s not a Qwen2.5 bug. Qwen2.5 just has less room for it.

Second, LoRA plus vLLM server mode means that at every sync, TRL merges the adapter into the base weights, ships the whole model over NCCL, and unmerges it. Hundreds of times per run. That’s the exact pattern in TRL #6688, where runs generating with Hugging Face and with vLLM diverge after the first epoch on bf16 LoRA.

TRL later added an adapter-only sync: send the adapter to vLLM without merging it into the base model (PR #7017). In a 500-step test, the trainer and vLLM stayed very close, with their ratio between 0.9998 and 1.0. That was a useful clue, but not a fix I could turn on: the new path was only in the experimental AsyncGRPOTrainer, and it landed after the TRL version I was using. Switching trainers would have changed my setup instead of explaining what was wrong with its sync. It also didn’t explain my fp32 run, where merging is exact.

So I kept the same trainer and tested full fine-tuning with vLLM. With no adapter to merge, it would tell me whether the drift was specific to the LoRA sync.

All bf16: SFT, then OPD, then RL

With RL finally working, I wanted to squeeze the most out of the model. The plan was a bit of a yolo run: SFT for the format, OPD on top for correctness, then RL without vLLM, all in bf16. After the OPD checkpoint that hated being converted to bf16, I wanted checkpoints that are trained in the same precision they run in.

While OPD was running, I got worried about the order. My teacher, the 7B, only gets 77% of its answers in exact format. OPD pulls the student toward the teacher, format habits included, so OPD after SFT could undo some of the format SFT had just taught. I kept the order anyway. In my earlier OPD run, Qwen2.5-0.5B was the student and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct was the teacher. After OPD, the student reached around 90% format, even though the teacher was at 77%. RL now fixes the remaining format errors in no time.

The bigger surprise was somewhere else. Here are the SFT (idj5wrml) and OPD (ht3y144u) runs next to their fp32 versions from before:

The bf16 SFT loss only got from 0.61 to 0.48; in fp32 it went to 0.27. bf16 stores weights with 8 bits of precision, so neighbouring values of a weight are about 0.8% apart. One Adam step at a learning rate of 1e-5 (or OPD’s 2e-6) is much smaller than that, so most updates round straight back to the old value. I had used bf16 for the trainable weights too, because I wanted the checkpoints to be trained in the same precision they’d run in. That was the mistake: the optimizer had no fp32 copy to preserve those small updates. I could have kept fp32 master weights and still used bf16 for the matmuls.

Quick reminder: mixed precision

There are two setups that often get called mixed precision:

  • Autocast: parameters stay in fp32. PyTorch runs selected operations, like matrix multiplies, in bf16 and keeps others in fp32. The optimizer updates the fp32 parameters, so those are already the master weights. No second copy is needed. PyTorch’s AMP docs
  • Bf16 weights: parameters themselves are stored in bf16. If the optimizer updates those directly, each update is rounded back to bf16. To preserve smaller updates, keep fp32 master weights and use bf16 for computation.

I used bf16 weights for these warm-ups, so I don’t think I kept fp32 master weights. Adam’s fp32 optimizer state, if present, is separate; it doesn’t keep an fp32 copy of the parameters.

The presample confirmed it: 1,660 questions 0/8 and 306 8/8. That’s about where the SFT-only model was (1,705 and 274), nowhere near the fp32 OPD model (861 and 1,497). Lesson learned: bf16 for the matmuls is fine, but keep fp32 master weights.

Entropy collapse

RL on top of it, 6rr1hcot, took off immediately. Within 15 steps the reward was at 4, and exact accuracy on training batches went from 54% to 74% in 50 steps. But look at the entropy:

0.42 at step 1, 0.26 at step 11, 0.11 by step 41. The model was getting very sure of itself very fast, and I stopped the run at step 50. A model that confident stops exploring. Every group turns into eight copies of the same answer, and from there on RL only sharpens what it already does. Looking back, gdi2sbor had the same problem, just slower: its entropy went from 0.33 to 0.10 over 200 steps.

Fighting the collapse

TRL 1.13 has a few levers for this, and I switched on three of them for the next run, 75nd1lv5:

  • Adaptive entropy bonus (from Skywork-OR1), with a target of 0.30. Whenever entropy drops below the target, an entropy bonus gets turned up a little each step, and it backs off once entropy recovers.
  • Clip-higher (from DAPO): each batch gets two updates instead of one, so PPO’s clipping finally does something (remember the clip ratio that was always 0), with a looser upper bound (0.28) so unlikely tokens can gain probability faster.
  • A lower learning rate, 1e-5 instead of 3e-5, because starting from a strong checkpoint, 3e-5 moves fast enough to collapse quickly.

A KL penalty back to the starting model is in reserve if that’s not enough.

Well, the entropy part worked. It dipped to 0.25 around step 35, the bonus kicked in, and it climbed back to 0.34 and stayed there. But that was the only thing that worked. Exact accuracy on training batches went from 50% to about 61% in the first 30 steps, sat there, and then slid back to 52% by step 100. 6rr1hcot, with no levers, had gone from 54% to 74% in 50 steps. And the clip ratio, the whole reason for doing two updates per batch, stayed at exactly 0 for the entire run. So I paid for twice the compute, and the clipping never happened.

I stopped it at step 100 and took all three levers out again. A model that explores and doesn’t learn is worse than one that collapses and learns. The collapse is still a problem, I just need a better way to fight it.

Also, by now the runs without vLLM were getting painful: 10 to 16 seconds a step, against about 4 with vLLM. If I wanted to try more things, and one long yolo run at the end, I needed the fast path back. So it was time to go back to the question I had parked: why does RL through vLLM not work?

Back to vLLM

Full fine-tuning with vLLM

The test I had parked was full fine-tuning with vLLM. No LoRA means no merge and unmerge at every sync: the trainer just ships its actual weights. If the drift goes away, the merge is the problem. If it stays, it’s something else in the loop.

I ran the full fine-tuning test as 7re5fbb2: fp32, lr 1e-6, with the same fp32 OPD model and data as i7yh9cby. Twenty steps were enough. By then, the mismatch in i7yh9cby had already grown to 60 times its starting value.

TRL’s sampling_logp_difference/mean is the average absolute difference between the trainer’s and vLLM’s log-probability for each sampled token. For each token, it takes the difference between the two log probabilities, drops the sign, then averages over the completion tokens. The logs are natural logs, so the unit is nats per token. Zero means the copies assigned the sampled token the same probability. (TRL docs)

The full fine-tuning line was flat: 0.0006 at step 1, 0.0007 at step 10, 0.0006 at step 20. Its importance-sampling ratio stayed at 1.00. LoRA over the same 20 steps went from 0.0006 to 0.036, while its ratio fell from 1.00 to 0.39. So the two copies stayed in sync with full fine-tuning, but drifted apart with LoRA.

There was one other possibility: maybe the full fine-tuning model barely moved at lr 1e-6. I compared its step-20 checkpoint with the starting model on the same tokens. That difference was 0.118 nats per token, about 200 times the trainer-vLLM mismatch. The model had changed; vLLM had kept up.

Full fine-tuning stayed in sync while LoRA drifted, so the problem was specific to the LoRA sync path. The adapter-only path avoided that path, but it didn’t tell me what was going wrong in the one I was running. My tests in Attempt 3 had checked each piece separately; none had followed the tensors through a live sync. I went back to the TRL and vLLM code and traced one update through both.

Finding the bug

The bug was in the handoff between the two libraries.

In TRL’s weight iterator, LoRA sync merges the adapter into the base weights, then yields each weight to vLLM. These aren’t snapshots: param.data points to the live tensor. After the last weight, TRL unmerges the adapter before the iterator is done.

vLLM collects those tensors into 1 GB chunks before copying each chunk into an NCCL send buffer. For the earlier chunks, it copies while TRL is paused at a yield, with the adapter still merged. For the last chunk, vLLM asks the iterator for another weight to see if there is more. TRL reaches the end and unmerges the adapter first. Then vLLM copies the last chunk. Those tensors now hold the plain base weights again.

Here’s one sync of the fp32 model:

How much of the model lands in that last chunk depends on how big the model is:

Model Size Chunks Stuck at the starting weights in vLLM
Qwen2.5-0.5B, bf16 0.99 GB 1 everything
Qwen2.5-0.5B, fp32 1.98 GB 2 layers 9–23 of 24
Qwen3-0.6B, bf16 1.19 GB 2 the last 4 of 28 layers

I checked it on CPU with TRL’s own generator and vLLM’s own packing function, on one of the step-100 adapters from the fp32 runs. In fp32, 63 of the 168 weight matrices LoRA touches reached vLLM with their update, and the other 105 arrived as base weights. In bf16, the share of the update that reached vLLM was -0.001. Basically zero.

And that explains everything at once:

  • Every bf16 Qwen2.5 run with vLLM, from jr8dtkxv to c0uc1sfx: vLLM never got a single LoRA update. For hundreds of steps, every rollout came from the starting model while the trainer moved on without it. The importance-sampling ratio fell because the gap between the two copies was literally the whole of training, and sequence_mask threw away more and more of every batch.
  • The fp32 run (i7yh9cby) drifted from step 1, because two thirds of the model in vLLM was frozen at the start and the gap grew with every update. That’s the 0.003 per step I kept staring at.
  • Qwen3 learned because only its last 4 layers were stuck. Most of the update got through, and its mismatch grew slowly, 0.012 to 0.029, which I had written off as bf16 noise.
  • Full fine-tuning was fine because there is no unmerge. The tensors vLLM holds are still the right weights when it copies them.
  • My piece-by-piece tests passed because in those, I merged the adapter myself, built the list of weights, and then synced. Nothing unmerged in the middle of the sync, so the bug never had a chance to happen. I had tested every piece, just not the order they run in.

So it wasn’t a config mistake on my side after all. TRL hands out live tensors it’s about to change, and vLLM’s packing assumes they won’t change until it copies them. Each one makes sense on its own, and together they break. As of today, it’s still the same on both TRL’s and vLLM’s main branches.

The fix

The fix is small: copy every tensor while the adapter is still merged, and hand vLLM the copies. The unmerge can do whatever it wants to the live weights after that. It costs one extra copy of the model on the GPU that sends, about 2 GB in fp32 for this model. I ran the CPU check again. In fp32, all 290 tensors now arrive exactly as the merged model. In bf16, 71% of the update gets through, and the rest is lost to rounding when a small update gets added to a bf16 weight (the same thing I saw in Attempt 3). No sync can fix that part.

Then I tried the fix live in wyua69fh: LoRA, fp32, vLLM, 20 steps. It started from the same model as i7yh9cby.

I added a probe too. After each sync, it scores the same 8 GSM8K test solutions with both copies. The usual mismatch is measured on that step’s sampled tokens, which change from step to step. The probe keeps the tokens fixed, so a change in the vLLM-trainer difference means the copies are drifting.

0.0006 at step 1 and 0.0006 at step 20, with the ratio between 0.998 and 1.005 the whole way. And the probe says the same thing from the other side: vLLM and the trainer stayed about 0.002 apart, while vLLM moved away from where it started, from 0 to 0.064 nats per token. For the first time, the vLLM copy was actually training along with the trainer.

The yolo run, finally fast

Quick reset: this is OPD warm-up, then RL. No SFT warm-up. The student was Qwen2.5-0.5B; for OPD, it learned from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on its own answers (3fjg9zef). Then I ran RL on the 3,763 questions left after the presample. The earlier run, i7yh9cby, used the same fp32 OPD model and data, but the LoRA sync bug meant vLLM missed part of each update. The 20-step test above, wyua69fh, showed the fix kept the two copies in sync. Now I wanted to see what happened over a full run: three epochs, about 800 steps, at 4 seconds a step (ss5zdsm3).

The mismatch stayed between 0.0005 and 0.0007 for all 208 steps, and the ratio at 1.00. The first Qwen2.5 run with vLLM where the two copies agreed from start to finish. Exact accuracy on training batches went from 66% in the first 25 steps to 80%, and on the test set, 52.9% at step 100 and 54.0% at step 200. i7yh9cby, same start before the fix: 47.9% and 48.4%.

The best Qwen2.5 number in this worklog, but it was flattening out, and the entropy was doing the same thing as before: 0.21 over the first 25 steps, 0.09 by step 200. Still well short of Qwen3’s 67.2%, so I stopped it at step 208.

And that 67.2% deserves an asterisk now. Qwen3 was trained through the same bug, with its last 4 layers stuck in vLLM the whole run. So it’s not even a fair baseline anymore.

bf16, now that the sync works

With the sync fixed, I wanted to know if the fix also saves bf16, the all-bf16 yolo plan from before: the bf16 SFT+OPD model, RL in bf16, but with vLLM this time. The CPU check had already warned me that bf16 only gets 71% of each update through, but I wanted to see what that does to a real run: hqn8qlkh, probe on.

It learned. Exact accuracy on training batches went from 60% to 79% in about 130 steps, and the test set came in at 45.7% at step 100 and 48.8% at step 200. The mismatch sat around 0.009 the whole run, which is just what two bf16 copies disagree by, and it didn’t climb.

But the probe told a different story:

In fp32, vLLM and the trainer stayed 0.002 apart. In bf16, they started 0.022 apart and drifted to 0.055. That’s the other 29% of every update getting rounded away, plus the trainer’s own base weights getting rounded a little more at every merge and unmerge. The importance-sampling ratio slid from 0.99 to 0.94 by the end. Not a disaster, but it’s the old problem again, just slower. And entropy went off a cliff: 0.26 at the start, 0.07 by step 110.

So for the last runs I kept the bf16 SFT+OPD model (its weights are bf16, so loading them in fp32 is exact), but ran RL in fp32.

One last yolo: SFT + OPD + RL, in fp32

All right, here’s the full stack: SFT → OPD → RL. The first time around, SFT and OPD were separate experiments. SFT got the format right; OPD gave a much bigger jump in exact accuracy. I wanted to see if I could get both: teach the student the format with SFT, then give it the 7B teacher’s reasoning with OPD, then let RL work on the questions still left. That’s the model behind this run.

The bf16 version reached 48.8%, but the probe showed the two copies drifting. So: same SFT+OPD model, same RL data, but fp32 for RL. And I saved a checkpoint every 10 steps instead of every 100. I had a trick in mind for all those checkpoints. This was cr17x4tb.
